01
Chapter one

Foundations

A test is code that runs your code and checks the answer. Good tests let you change software quickly without breaking it; bad ones slow you down and still let bugs through. This chapter covers what to test, how much of each kind, and how to pick the cases.

What tests buy you

Fast feedback

Find a mistake seconds after you make it, not weeks later in production.

Safe change

Refactor or upgrade a library and know at once whether behaviour changed.

Living docs

A test named declinedPaymentSavesNothing states a rule that can’t go out of date.

Better design

Testing a class in isolation needs its dependencies passed in, which keeps coupling visible.

The kinds of tests

KindWhat it checksScopeSpeedJava tools
staticCode style, likely bugs, types — without running anythingWhole code baseSecondsjavac -Xlint, Error Prone, SpotBugs, Checkstyle · p.44, p.45
unitOne class or function; collaborators replaced by doublesSingle process, no I/OMillisecondsJUnit, AssertJ, Mockito · p.08, p.14
integrationYour code with real neighbours: DB, HTTP, queue, frameworkProcess + real dependenciesSub-second to secondsSpring Boot test slices, Testcontainers, WireMock · p.19, p.30
contractConsumer and provider agree on the API shapeTwo services, one at a timeSecondsPact, Spring Cloud Contract · p.31
end-to-endA user journey through the deployed systemBrowser / client → all servicesSeconds to minutesPlaywright, Selenium, REST Assured · p.34
performanceLatency, throughput and limits under loadProduction-like environmentMinutes to hoursGatling, JMeter, k6, JMH · p.35
securityKnown weaknesses, vulnerable libraries, attack pathsCode, dependencies, running appMinutesZAP, OWASP Dependency-Check, Jazzer · p.36, p.29
Good to knowGoogle’s Software Engineering at Google sorts tests by size instead of name: small tests run in one process, medium tests on one machine (they may call localhost), large tests anywhere. The book’s reason: “the most important qualities we want from our test suite are speed and determinism”, and “small tests, regardless of the scope, are almost always faster and more deterministic”.

Vocabulary

SUTSystem under test — the class or system being tested.
FixtureEverything set up so a test can run.
AssertionA check that fails the test if it is false.
Test doubleA stand-in for a real collaborator.
RegressionSomething that used to work and broke.
Flaky testPasses and fails without any code change.
Test oracleHow you know the expected answer.
Smoke testA quick check that the build basically works.
Acceptance testChecks a requirement from the user’s view.
CoverageWhich code the tests executed.
Mutation scoreShare of injected bugs the tests caught.
Test suiteA group of tests run together.

01 · Foundations

Pyramid, trophy & what makes a good test

The pyramid says: write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a handful of end-to-end tests, because cost and flakiness grow as you go up. Mike Cohn described it in Succeeding with Agile (2009).

The trophy (Kent C. Dodds, first drawn in a 2018 tweet) puts the most weight on integration tests, with static analysis as the base. Its premise: “The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you.”

FIRST: five properties of a good unit test

FFastMilliseconds. Slow tests stop being run.
IIndependentNo shared state; any order, in parallel.
RRepeatableSame result anywhere: no real clock, network or randomness.
SSelf-validatingPass or fail by itself; nobody reads logs.
TTimelyWritten with (or before) the code, not months later.

Mnemonic devised by Brett Schuchert and Tim Ottinger; listed in chapter 9 of Robert C. Martin’s Clean Code.

Arrange · Act · Assert

MoneyTest.java✔ passes
@Test
@DisplayName("10% off ₹999.99 rounds half-up to ₹899.99")
void percentOffRoundsHalfUp() {
  Money price = Money.of("999.99");  // Arrange

  Money discounted = price.percentOff(10);  // Act

  assertEquals(Money.of("899.99"), discounted); // Assert
}

Three blocks, separated by blank lines. Given / When / Then is the same idea in BDD words. If “Act” needs more than one line, the API under test is probably awkward.

Naming tests

StyleExample
Behaviour sentencedeclinedPaymentSavesNothingAndSendsNoEmail
method_state_resultplaceOrder_emptyItems_throws
should…shouldRejectNegativeAmounts
@DisplayName"10% off ₹999.99 rounds half-up"
Do
  • Test behaviour through the public API
  • One reason to fail per test
  • Make failures explain themselves
Don’t
  • Assert on private fields or call order you don’t care about
  • Share mutable state between tests
  • Put if or loops with logic in a test

01 · Foundations

What to test — and what to leave out

Testing everything equally is the most expensive way to get mediocre safety. Spend tests where a bug would hurt most, write each one so it is worth keeping, and pick the cheapest kind of test that can catch the bug you are worried about.

Four properties of a valuable test

Catches regressionsFails when behaviour breaks. More real code exercised, more bugs caught.
Survives refactoringStays green when behaviour doesn’t change. Tests tied to internals fail for nothing — and get ignored.
Fast feedbackRuns in milliseconds, so it runs on every change.
Cheap to keepEasy to read, small setup, one reason to fail.

From Vladimir Khorikov, Unit Testing: Principles, Practices, and Patterns (2020). Khorikov’s names: protection against regressions, resistance to refactoring, fast feedback, maintainability; he argues the first three can’t all be maximised at once. To keep a test resistant to refactoring, assert on outcomes (return values, saved state, messages sent), not on which private steps produced them.

Test by risk

CodeRiskHow much testing
Money, permissions, personal datahighunit tests for every rule and boundary, mutation testing, an integration test per path, a contract per consumer
Core business ruleshighunit tests with boundaries and decision tables; PIT on the module
Wiring: SQL, HTTP, messaging, configmediumintegration tests with the real thing in a container
User journeys that earn moneymediuma few end-to-end tests: sign-up, checkout, payment
Glue code that only delegateslowcovered by the integration test above it — no unit test of its own
Getters, generated code, the framework itselfnonedon’t test; it is someone else’s job or has no logic

Which test catches which bug

The bug you fearCheapest testPage
A rule computes the wrong numberunit testp.06
SQL or mapping is wrongintegration testp.19
Schema change breaks old datamigration testp.21
Another service is slow or downWireMock stubp.30
An API change breaks a consumercontract testp.31
A duplicate message is applied twiceintegration testp.26
The wrong user can see an ordersecurity + auth testsp.29
Layers get tangled over timearchitecture testp.45
The checkout button stops workingend-to-end testp.34
It is too slow under loadperformance testp.35

Assert the outcome, not the steps

BehaviourFragile: tied to how it worksRobust: checks what it does
Order totalverify discountPolicy.percentFor() was called onceassert the total is ₹1,140.00
Order savedverify the exact SQL string sent to the databaseread the order back and check its fields
E-mail sentverify a private formatBody() helper ranassert the received mail’s recipient and subject
Payment before saving— (here the order of calls is the rule)InOrder: charge, then save (p.15)

Interaction checks are right when the interaction is the behaviour — a payment charged, an e-mail requested, a message published — and wrong when they pin down internal steps.

Rule of thumbBefore writing a test, ask: what bug would this catch, and is there a cheaper test that catches it already? If you can’t name the bug, the test is probably testing the framework, the language — or nothing.

Designing test cases

You can’t test every input, so pick the few that are most likely to find bugs. The rule: DiscountPolicy gives 0% below ₹1000, 5% from ₹1000 and 10% from ₹5000.

DiscountPolicyTest.java
@ParameterizedTest(name = "₹{0} → {1}% off",
                   quoteTextArguments = false)
@CsvSource({
  "0,       0",
  "999.99,  0",  // just below the first boundary
  "1000,    5",  // on the boundary
  "1000.01, 5",
  "4999.99, 5",
  "5000,   10",  // on the second boundary
  "250000, 10"
}
test output · JUnit 6.1.37 / 7 passed
└─ percentForSubtotal(String, int) ✔
   ├─ ₹0 → 0% off ✔
   ├─ ₹999.99 → 0% off ✔
   ├─ ₹1000 → 5% off ✔
   ├─ ₹1000.01 → 5% off ✔
   ├─ ₹4999.99 → 5% off ✔
   ├─ ₹5000 → 10% off ✔
   └─ ₹250000 → 10% off ✔

Mistype >= as > and only the ₹1000 row fails — see the mutation demo on p.39. Middle-of-range values like ₹2000 would never notice.

Decision table for placeOrder

Rule1234
Items present?noyesyesyes
Payment approved?—noyesyes
Subtotal ≥ ₹1000?——noyes
Outcomereject, call nobodythrow, save nothingsave, email, 0%save, email, 5–10%
TestemptyOrderIsRejected…declinedPayment…chargesBeforeSavingchargesDiscounted…

Test design techniques

TechniqueHowBest for
Equivalence partitioningSplit inputs into groups the code treats the same; test one value from each.Fewer tests, same coverage of behaviour
Boundary value analysisTest on and either side of every edge: 999.99, 1000, 1000.01.Catches off-by-one and > vs >=
Decision tableList every combination of conditions and the expected action.Business rules with several inputs
State transitionTest each allowed move between states — and the forbidden ones.Orders, payments, workflows
PairwiseCover every pair of option values instead of every combination.Config and browser/OS matrices
Property-basedState a rule (“total ≥ 0”) and let a tool generate hundreds of inputs.Parsers, maths, serialisation (jqwik)
Error guessingUse experience: null, empty, huge, Unicode, duplicates, time zones.Finds what specs forget

Inputs worth trying on almost anything

Empty & missingnull, "", empty list, missing JSON field, zero items.
Extremes0, -1, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 10 MB strings, 10,000 rows.
TextUnicode (₹, emoji, Hindi), leading spaces, mixed case, SQL and HTML characters.
TimeMidnight, 29 Feb, month end, DST change, a different time zone.

Chapter two

Unit testing with JUnit 6

JUnit is the standard test framework for Java. Version 6 (30 September 2025) keeps the JUnit 5 programming model — the org.junit.jupiter API — and raises the floor to Java 17. Every test in this guide ran on JUnit 6.1.3, Mockito 5.24.0 and AssertJ 3.27.7 on Java 21.

How the pieces fit

Maven

pom.xml — test dependencies
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-bom</artifactId>
      <version>6.1.3</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.assertj</groupId>
    <artifactId>assertj-core</artifactId>
    <version>3.27.7</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.mockito</groupId>
    <artifactId>mockito-junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.24.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Gradle (Kotlin DSL)

build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
  testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3"))
  testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
  testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")
  testImplementation("org.assertj:assertj-core:3.27.7")
  testImplementation("org.mockito:mockito-junit-jupiter:5.24.0")
}

tasks.test {
  useJUnitPlatform()
}

Coming from JUnit 4

JUnit 4JUnit 5 / 6
@Before / @After@BeforeEach / @AfterEach
@BeforeClass / @AfterClass@BeforeAll / @AfterAll
@Ignore@Disabled
@Category(Slow.class)@Tag("slow")
@RunWith(…)@ExtendWith(…)
@Rule / @ClassRule@ExtendWith or @RegisterExtension
@Test(expected = X.class)assertThrows(X.class, …)
@Test(timeout = 500)@Timeout(value = 500, unit = MILLISECONDS)
assertEquals(msg, exp, act)assertEquals(exp, act, msg) — message last
public class / public voidpackage-private is enough

junit-jupiter bundles the API, the parameterized-test module and the engine. mockito-junit-jupiter brings mockito-core with it. Run with mvn test or ./gradlew test; one class with mvn test -Dtest=MoneyTest.

02 · Unit testing with JUnit 6

Your first test & the lifecycle

MoneyTest.java✔ 3 / 3 passed
class MoneyTest {

  @Test
  @DisplayName("10% off ₹999.99 rounds half-up to ₹899.99")
  void percentOffRoundsHalfUp() {
    Money price = Money.of("999.99");  // Arrange

    Money discounted = price.percentOff(10);  // Act

    assertEquals(Money.of("899.99"), discounted); // Assert
  }

  @Test
  void rejectsNegativeAmounts() {
    var error = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> Money.of("-1"));
    assertEquals("negative amount: -1", error.getMessage());
  }

  // addsAndMultiplies() is shown on p.09
}

The class under test is a small Money record (₹, two decimals). Test classes and methods can be package-private; JUnit finds any method annotated with @Test.

The annotations you’ll use daily

@TestA test method. No return value, not private.
@ParameterizedTestRuns once per set of arguments (see p.10).
@BeforeEach / @AfterEachRun around every test: fresh fixtures, clean-up.
@BeforeAll / @AfterAllOnce per class; static unless @TestInstance(PER_CLASS).
@DisplayNameReadable name in reports, any text or emoji.
@NestedInner class that groups related tests and shares setup.
@Tag("slow")Label for filtering what runs, e.g. in CI stages.
@Disabled("why")Skip, with a reason. Prefer fixing or deleting.
@TempDirInject a fresh temporary directory, deleted afterwards.
@ExtendWithPlug in an extension, e.g. MockitoExtension.

Lifecycle, observed

LifecycleTest.java
class LifecycleTest {
  static void log(String s) { System.out.println(s); }

  LifecycleTest() { log("  new LifecycleTest()"); }

  @BeforeAll static void beforeAll() { log("@BeforeAll"); }
  @BeforeEach void beforeEach()      { log("  @BeforeEach"); }

  @Test void first()                 { log("    first()"); }
  @Test void second()                { log("    second()"); }

  @AfterEach void afterEach()        { log("  @AfterEach"); }
  @AfterAll static void afterAll()   { log("@AfterAll"); }
}
real output
@BeforeAll
  new LifecycleTest()
  @BeforeEach
    second()
  @AfterEach
  new LifecycleTest()
  @BeforeEach
    first()
  @AfterEach
@AfterAll
  • A new instance per test method, so fields can’t leak state between tests.
  • Order is deterministic but deliberately not obvious — here second() ran first. Never depend on it.
  • Need an order? @TestMethodOrder(OrderAnnotation.class) — mostly for slow, staged integration tests.
  • @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) reuses one instance, so @BeforeAll need not be static.

What changed in JUnit 6

ChangeWhat it means for you
Java 17 minimumProjects on older JDKs stay on JUnit 5.14.x until they upgrade.
One version for everythingPlatform, Jupiter and Vintage now share one number, so the BOM is simpler.
Vintage deprecatedJUnit 4 tests still run, but the engine flags them at discovery; plan the migration.
Quoted text argumentsParameterized names show "1000"; turn off with quoteTextArguments = false.
CSV parsing via FastCSV@CsvSource is stricter: characters after a closing quote are now an error.

02 · Unit testing with JUnit 6

Assertions & AssertJ

An assertion is the test’s oracle. JUnit’s Assertions class covers the basics; AssertJ adds a fluent style — type assertThat(x). and your IDE lists every check that makes sense for x — and much clearer failure messages.

JUnit assertions

assertEquals(expected, actual)Uses equals(). Expected first!
assertTrue / assertFalseFor booleans; message explains little.
assertNull / assertNotNullNull checks.
assertSameSame object reference (==).
assertIterableEqualsSame elements, same order.
assertThrows(Type, code)Returns the exception for further checks.
assertThrowsExactlyExact type, not a subclass.
assertDoesNotThrowDocuments that code must not fail.
assertAll(…)Runs every check and reports all failures.
assertTimeout(Preemptively)Fails when slower than a limit.
assertInstanceOfType check that returns the cast value.

Exceptions and grouped checks

MoneyTest.java✔ both pass
@Test
void rejectsNegativeAmounts() {
  var error = assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
      () -> Money.of("-1"));
  assertEquals("negative amount: -1", error.getMessage());
}

@Test
void addsAndMultiplies() {
  Money m = Money.of("12.50");
  assertAll("arithmetic",
      () -> assertEquals(Money.of("25.00"), m.plus(m)),
      () -> assertEquals(Money.of("37.50"), m.times(3)),
      () -> assertEquals("₹12.50", m.toString()));
}

The same ideas in AssertJ

ItemTest.java
void rejected(int qty) {
  assertThatThrownBy(() -> new Item("SKU-1", Money.of("10"), qty))
    .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("quantity");
}

Failure messages are the real product

A test earns its keep the day it fails. These are the exact messages JUnit and AssertJ printed when we broke an expectation on purpose:

assertEquals
assertEquals(Money.of("900.00"),
    Money.of("999.99").percentOff(10));
JUnit says
expected: <₹900.00> but was: <₹899.99>
assertAll
assertAll("arithmetic",
  () -> assertEquals(Money.of("25.00"), m.times(3)),
  () -> assertEquals("Rs 12.50", m.toString()));
JUnit says — both failures
arithmetic (2 failures)
  AssertionFailedError: expected: <₹25.00> but was: <₹37.50>
  AssertionFailedError: expected: <Rs 12.50> but was: <₹12.50>
AssertJ
assertThat(List.of("PEN", "BOOK", "TV"))
    .containsExactly("PEN", "TV", "BOOK");
AssertJ says
Expecting actual:
  ["PEN", "BOOK", "TV"]
to contain exactly (and in same order):
  ["PEN", "TV", "BOOK"]
but there were differences at these indexes:
  - element at index 1: expected "TV" but was "BOOK"
  - element at index 2: expected "BOOK" but was "TV"
Watch outPut expected first in assertEquals(expected, actual). Swapped arguments still fail correctly, but the message lies about which value was wrong. AssertJ avoids the problem: assertThat(actual).isEqualTo(expected).
TipCompare money with BigDecimal and a fixed scale. new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false; that’s why Money always calls setScale(2).

02 · Unit testing with JUnit 6

Parameterized, nested & more

When several tests differ only in their data, write one parameterized test. Each row becomes its own entry in the report, so you see exactly which case failed.

ItemTest.java — @Nested + @MethodSource + @ValueSource
@DisplayName("Item")
class ItemTest {

  @Nested @DisplayName("when quantity is valid")
  class ValidQuantity {
    @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} × ₹{1} = ₹{2}",
             quoteTextArguments = false)
    @MethodSource("shop.ItemTest#totals")
    void totalIsPriceTimesQty(int qty, String price, String total) {
      assertThat(new Item("SKU-1", Money.of(price), qty).total())
        .isEqualTo(Money.of(total));
    }
  }

  @Nested @DisplayName("when quantity is invalid")
  class InvalidQuantity {
    @ParameterizedTest(name = "quantity {0} is rejected")
    @ValueSource(ints = {0, -1, Integer.MIN_VALUE})
    void rejected(int qty) {
      assertThatThrownBy(() -> new Item("SKU-1", Money.of("10"), qty))
        .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class)
        .hasMessageContaining("quantity");
    }
  }

  static Stream<Arguments> totals() {
    return Stream.of(
      Arguments.of(1, "10", "10"),
      Arguments.of(3, "19.99", "59.97"),
      Arguments.of(1000, "0.01", "10"));
  }
}
real output6 / 6 passed
Item ✔
├─ when quantity is invalid ✔
│  └─ rejected(int) ✔
│     ├─ quantity 0 is rejected ✔
│     ├─ quantity -1 is rejected ✔
│     └─ quantity -2147483648 is rejected ✔
└─ when quantity is valid ✔
   └─ totalIsPriceTimesQty(int, String, String) ✔
      ├─ 1 × ₹10 = ₹10 ✔
      ├─ 3 × ₹19.99 = ₹59.97 ✔
      └─ 1000 × ₹0.01 = ₹10 ✔
JUnit 6 changeJUnit 6 prints text arguments in quotes, and @CsvSource values count as text — even numbers. quoteTextArguments = false keeps names like ₹1000 → 5% off.
Rule of thumbKeep each row one behaviour. If rows need different assertions, they are different tests.

Argument sources

@ValueSource(ints = {0, -1})One literal argument per run
@NullAndEmptySourceAdds null and ""/empty collection
@EnumSource(Status.class)Every enum constant, or a filtered set
@CsvSource({"a, 1"})Several arguments per row, inline
@CsvFileSource("/cases.csv")Rows from a CSV file on the classpath
@MethodSource("cases")A static factory returning Stream<Arguments>
@FieldSource("cases")A static field holding the arguments (JUnit 5.11+)
@ArgumentsSource(My.class)Your own reusable ArgumentsProvider

More tools in the box

Tags & filtering@Tag("slow") on a class or method, then mvn test -Dgroups=fast or -DexcludedGroups=slow.
AssumptionsassumeTrue(isCi()) aborts (skips) the test instead of failing it when a precondition doesn’t hold.
Conditional tests@EnabledOnOs(LINUX), @EnabledForJreRange(min = JAVA_21), @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable.
Timeouts@Timeout(5) on a method or class; assertTimeoutPreemptively for one block (see p.32).
Temp files@TempDir Path dir gives each test a fresh folder and deletes it afterwards.
Extensions@ExtendWith / @RegisterExtension hook into the lifecycle: Mockito, Spring, Testcontainers all work this way.

02 · Unit testing with JUnit 6

Writing your own JUnit extensions

When the same setup appears in many test classes — a fixed clock, a timer, a test database — turn it into an extension. Extensions plug into the test lifecycle through small interfaces; a composed annotation then gives the whole team one line to write.

FixedClockExtension — a ParameterResolver
/** Resolves a Clock parameter from @FixedClock on the test. */
public class FixedClockExtension implements ParameterResolver {
  @Override
  public boolean supportsParameter(ParameterContext p,
      ExtensionContext ctx) {
    return p.getParameter().getType() == Clock.class;
  }

  @Override
  public Object resolveParameter(ParameterContext p,
      ExtensionContext ctx) {
    FixedClock fixed = AnnotationSupport.findAnnotation(
            ctx.getRequiredTestMethod(), FixedClock.class)
        .or(() -> AnnotationSupport.findAnnotation(
            ctx.getRequiredTestClass(), FixedClock.class))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new ParameterResolutionException(
            "Clock parameter needs @FixedClock"));
    return Clock.fixed(Instant.parse(fixed.value()),
        ZoneOffset.UTC);
  }
}
TimingExtension — lifecycle callbacks + the Store
/** Reports how long each test method took. */
public class TimingExtension implements
    BeforeTestExecutionCallback, AfterTestExecutionCallback {
  private static final Namespace NS =
      Namespace.create(TimingExtension.class);

  @Override
  public void beforeTestExecution(ExtensionContext ctx) {
    ctx.getStore(NS).put("start", System.nanoTime());
  }

  @Override
  public void afterTestExecution(ExtensionContext ctx) {
    long start = ctx.getStore(NS).remove("start", Long.class);
    long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
    System.out.printf("[timing] %s took %d ms%n",
        ctx.getDisplayName(), ms);
  }
}
ShopTest — a composed annotation
/** One annotation for the team: tag + both extensions. */
DeliveryDateTest — using it
@ShopTest
@FixedClock("2026-10-16T09:00:00Z")          // a Friday
class DeliveryDateTest {

  /** Ships in 2 working days; weekends don't count. */
  static LocalDate deliveryDate(Clock clock) {
    LocalDate day = LocalDate.now(clock);
    for (int left = 2; left > 0; ) {
      day = day.plusDays(1);
      if (day.getDayOfWeek().getValue() < 6) left--;
    }
    return day;
  }

  @Test
  void fridayOrderArrivesTuesday(Clock clock) {
    assertThat(deliveryDate(clock)).isEqualTo("2026-10-20");
  }

  // … @RepeatedTest(3), TestInfo — see the repo
}
real output · Surefire 3.6.0
[timing] fridayOrderArrivesTuesday(Clock) took 4 ms
[timing] repetition 1 of 3 took 2 ms
[timing] repetition 2 of 3 took 0 ms
[timing] repetition 3 of 3 took 0 ms
[timing] tuesdayOrderArrivesThursday(Clock, TestInfo) took 1 ms
Tests run: 5, Failures: 0

Extension points you will use

InterfaceUse it to
BeforeAllCallback, BeforeEachCallback, …TestExecutionCallback, After…set up and tear down around tests — like @BeforeEach, but reusable
ParameterResolverinject arguments into test methods and constructors
ExecutionConditiondecide whether a test runs at all
TestExecutionExceptionHandlerreact to — or swallow — exceptions thrown by tests
TestWatcherhear about results: passed, failed, aborted, disabled
InvocationInterceptorwrap the call itself, e.g. run it on another thread
  • Register with @ExtendWith (as above), a static @RegisterExtension field when you need to configure it, or automatically through ServiceLoader with junit.jupiter.extensions.autodetection.enabled=true.
  • Keep state in the ExtensionContext.Store, never in fields: one extension instance serves many tests, possibly in parallel.
  • TestInfo and RepetitionInfo are built-in parameter resolvers — that is how @RepeatedTest tells you which run it is.
  • Look for an existing extension first: Mockito, Spring, Testcontainers and many libraries ship one.

02 · Unit testing with JUnit 6

Testing logs and metrics

On-call engineers read your log lines, and alerts fire on your metrics. If a refactoring silently drops a warning or renames a counter, production monitoring goes blind — so assert on them like any other output.

PaymentService.java
public class PaymentService {
  private static final Logger log =
      LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class);
  static final long LIMIT_PAISE = 5_000_000;     // ₹50,000

  private final Counter declined;

  public PaymentService(MeterRegistry registry) {
    declined = Counter.builder("payments.declined")
        .tag("reason", "over_limit")
        .register(registry);
  }

  public boolean charge(String orderId, long amountPaise) {
    if (amountPaise > LIMIT_PAISE) {
      declined.increment();
      log.warn("Payment declined for order {}: over limit",
          orderId);
      return false;
    }
    log.info("Charged order {}", orderId);
    return true;
  }
}
PaymentServiceTest — Logback ListAppender + Micrometer2 ✔ · 0.056 s
class PaymentServiceTest {
  SimpleMeterRegistry registry = new SimpleMeterRegistry();
  ListAppender<ILoggingEvent> logs = new ListAppender<>();
  Logger logger =
      (Logger) LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class);

  @BeforeEach void capture() {
    logs.start();
    logger.addAppender(logs);
  }
  @AfterEach void release() { logger.detachAppender(logs); }

  @Test
  void declinedPaymentIsLoggedAndCounted() {
    var payments = new PaymentService(registry);

    assertThat(payments.charge("ord-9", 6_000_000)).isFalse();

    assertThat(logs.list)
        .extracting(ILoggingEvent::getLevel,
                    ILoggingEvent::getFormattedMessage)
        .containsExactly(tuple(Level.WARN,
            "Payment declined for order ord-9: over limit"));
    assertThat(registry.get("payments.declined")
        .tag("reason", "over_limit").counter().count())
        .isEqualTo(1.0);
  }

  @Test
  void normalPaymentRaisesNoAlarm() {
    var payments = new PaymentService(registry);

    assertThat(payments.charge("ord-1", 100_000)).isTrue();

    assertThat(logs.list)
        .noneMatch(e -> e.getLevel() == Level.WARN);
    assertThat(registry.get("payments.declined")
        .counter().count()).isZero();
  }
}
Logs: capture, don’t parse filesAttach Logback’s ListAppender to the logger under test and assert on level and message. Detach it afterwards so tests stay independent.
Metrics: a real registryMicrometer’s SimpleMeterRegistry is an in-memory registry made for tests. Assert on the meter name and tags your dashboards and alerts use.

Tools for each signal

SignalTest toolAssert on
Logs (Logback)ListAppender attached to the loggerlevel, message or key, MDC values
Logs (Spring Boot)OutputCaptureExtension → CapturedOutputtext written to stdout / stderr
Metrics (Micrometer)SimpleMeterRegistrymeter name, tags, count or total
Traces (OpenTelemetry)InMemorySpanExporter from opentelemetry-sdk-testingspan names, attributes, parent/child links
Rule of thumbAssert on what operators depend on — level, a stable message or key, metric name and tags — not on whole formatted lines with timestamps. Otherwise every log-format change breaks tests.

03
Chapter three

Test doubles & Mockito

A unit test shouldn’t send real e-mails or charge real cards. A test double stands in for a collaborator, like a stunt double for an actor. The five kinds come from Gerard Meszaros’s xUnit Test Patterns (2007).

The five test doubles

DoubleWhat it isWhat you verifyIn this guide
dummyFills a parameter list; never actually used.NothingdummyEmail throws if touched
stubReturns canned answers to calls.State of the SUTalwaysApproves payment gateway
spyA stub that also records the calls it got.Behaviour, checked by youSpyEmailSender.sentTo
mockPre-programmed with expectations; the library checks them.BehaviourMockito verify(email).send(…)
fakeA working, simplified implementation.State, realisticallyInMemoryOrderRepository
TestDoublesTest.java — no library needed✔ 3 / 3 passed
/** The five kinds of test double, hand-written — no library needed. */
class TestDoublesTest {

  // DUMMY: passed in to satisfy a parameter, never used
  EmailSender dummyEmail = (to, subject, body) -> {
    throw new AssertionError("not used");
  };

  // STUB: returns canned answers
  PaymentGateway alwaysApproves = (customer, amount) -> "PAY-1";

  // SPY: a stub that also records how it was called
  static class SpyEmailSender implements EmailSender {
    final List<String> sentTo = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override public void send(String to, String subject, String body) {
      sentTo.add(to);
    }
  }

  // FAKE: a real but simplified implementation (a map instead of a DB)
  OrderRepository fakeRepo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();

  List<Item> pens = List.of(new Item("PEN", Money.of("50"), 2));

  OrderService serviceWith(EmailSender email) {
    return new OrderService(fakeRepo, alwaysApproves, email,
        new DiscountPolicy(), Clock.systemUTC());
  }

  @Test
  void stubAndFakeLetUsCheckState() {
    var service = serviceWith(new SpyEmailSender());
    Order order = service.placeOrder("meera@example.com", pens);
    assertThat(fakeRepo.findById(order.id())).contains(order);  // state
  }

  @Test
  void spyLetsUsCheckBehaviour() {
    var spy = new SpyEmailSender();
    serviceWith(spy).placeOrder("meera@example.com", pens);
    assertThat(spy.sentTo)
        .containsExactly("meera@example.com");  // behaviour
  }

  @Test
  void dummyIsNeverTouchedWhenValidationFails() {
    var service = serviceWith(dummyEmail);
    assertThatIllegalArgumentException()
      .isThrownBy(() -> service.placeOrder("x@example.com", List.of()));
  }
}

State or behaviour?

State verification

Run the code, then look at the result: what was returned, or what is now stored in the fake. Survives refactoring well, because it doesn’t care how the result was reached.

Behaviour verification

Check which calls were made to collaborators: “an e-mail was sent to Meera”. Needed when the call is the result — sending, publishing, charging — and nothing observable is stored.

03 · Test doubles & Mockito

Mockito in practice

placeOrder applies the discount, charges the card, saves the order and e-mails the customer. In the test the gateway, repository and mailer are mocks; the clock is fixed.

OrderService.java — under test
public Order placeOrder(String customerEmail, List<Item> items) {
  if (items.isEmpty())
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("order has no items");
  Money subtotal = items.stream().map(Item::total)
      .reduce(Money.of("0"), Money::plus);
  Money total = subtotal.percentOff(discounts.percentFor(subtotal));
  payments.charge(customerEmail, total);  // may throw PaymentDeclined…
  Order order = repository.save(new Order(UUID.randomUUID().toString(),
      customerEmail, List.copyOf(items), total, clock.instant()));
  email.send(customerEmail, "Order confirmed", "Total: " + total);
  return order;
}
  • Every collaborator arrives through the constructor, so a test can pass in doubles — no framework needed.
  • Time comes from an injected java.time.Clock, so the timestamp is predictable.
  • placeOrder has one happy path and two failure paths: no items, or a declined card.
OrderServiceTest.java (first test)
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

  @Mock OrderRepository repository;
  @Mock PaymentGateway payments;
  @Mock EmailSender email;
  @Captor ArgumentCaptor<Order> savedOrder;

  Clock clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z"),
                            ZoneOffset.UTC);
  OrderService service;

  @BeforeEach
  void setUp() {
    service = new OrderService(repository, payments, email,
        new DiscountPolicy(), clock);
  }

  @Test
  void chargesDiscountedTotalSavesAndEmails() {
    when(repository.save(any())).thenAnswer(c -> c.getArgument(0));

    Order order = service.placeOrder("asha@example.com",
        List.of(new Item("BOOK", Money.of("600"), 2))); // ₹1200 → 5%

    assertThat(order.total()).isEqualTo(Money.of("1140"));
    verify(payments).charge("asha@example.com", Money.of("1140"));
    verify(repository).save(savedOrder.capture());
    assertThat(savedOrder.getValue().placedAt())
        .isEqualTo(clock.instant());
    verify(email).send(eq("asha@example.com"), eq("Order confirmed"),
        contains("₹1140.00"));
  }
real output4 / 4 passed
OrderServiceTest ✔
├─ chargesBeforeSaving() ✔
├─ chargesDiscountedTotalSavesAndEmails() ✔
├─ declinedPaymentSavesNothingAndSendsNoEmail() ✔
└─ emptyOrderIsRejectedEarly() ✔
  • @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) creates the @Mock and @Captor fields before each test and checks for unused stubs after it.
  • thenAnswer makes save return its argument, like a real repository.
  • ArgumentCaptor grabs the saved Order so we can check its timestamp came from the fixed clock.
  • eq and contains are matchers: one matcher means all arguments need one.
Constructor beats @InjectMocks@InjectMocks builds the object by constructor, setter or field injection — and fails silently if it can’t. Calling the constructor yourself is explicit and breaks loudly.
Defaults of a mockAn unstubbed mock returns empty values: null, 0, false, empty collections and Optional.empty(). Void methods simply do nothing.
Stub less, verify lessStub only what the code path needs and verify only calls that are the point of the test — the rest is noise that breaks on refactors.
Classicist

Use real objects where possible, doubles only for awkward ones (network, time, mail).

vs
Mockist

Use a mock for any collaborator with interesting behaviour, and verify the calls made to it.

From Martin Fowler’s Mocks Aren’t Stubs (2004, revised 2007).
Good to knowMockito’s mock() can be a stub, spy or mock depending on use — the library blurs Meszaros’s names. The five kinds still help you decide what to check.

03 · Test doubles & Mockito

Failure paths, call order & the API

OrderServiceTest.java — failure path and call order
@Test
void declinedPaymentSavesNothingAndSendsNoEmail() {
  when(payments.charge(anyString(), any()))
    .thenThrow(new PaymentDeclinedException("card expired"));

  assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.placeOrder("asha@example.com",
      List.of(new Item("PEN", Money.of("50"), 1))))
    .isInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedException.class)
    .hasMessage("card expired");

  verifyNoInteractions(repository, email);
}

@Test
void chargesBeforeSaving() {
  when(repository.save(any())).thenAnswer(c -> c.getArgument(0));

  service.placeOrder("asha@example.com",
      List.of(new Item("PEN", Money.of("50"), 1)));

  InOrder inOrder = inOrder(payments, repository, email);
  inOrder.verify(payments).charge(any(), any());
  inOrder.verify(repository).save(any());
  inOrder.verify(email).send(any(), any(), any());
}

The API on one table

Createmock(X.class) · @Mock · spy(obj) · @Spy · @Captor · @InjectMocks
Stubwhen(m.call()).thenReturn(v) · .thenThrow(e) · .thenAnswer(inv -> …)
Stub void / spiesdoThrow(e).when(m).call() · doReturn(v).when(spy).call() · doNothing()
Verifyverify(m).call() · times(2) · never() · atLeastOnce() · timeout(100) · verifyNoInteractions(m)
OrderInOrder o = inOrder(a, b); o.verify(a).x(); o.verify(b).y();
Matchany() · anyString() · eq(v) · contains(s) · argThat(x -> …) · isNull()
Captureverify(m).save(captor.capture()); captor.getValue()
BDD stylegiven(m.call()).willReturn(v) · then(m).should().call()

Given / when / then with BDDMockito

OrderServiceBddTest.java✔ passes
  @Test
  void bigOrderGetsTenPercentOff() {
    // given
    given(repository.save(any())).willAnswer(c -> c.getArgument(0));
    var service = new OrderService(repository, payments, email,
        new DiscountPolicy(), Clock.systemUTC());

    // when
    Order order = service.placeOrder("ravi@example.com",
        List.of(new Item("TV", Money.of("5000"), 1)));

    // then
    assertThat(order.total()).isEqualTo(Money.of("4500"));
    then(payments).should().charge("ravi@example.com", Money.of("4500"));
    then(email).should(times(1)).send(any(), any(), any());
  }
}

BDDMockito renames the same calls so tests read like a specification: given(…).willReturn(…) instead of when(…).thenReturn(…), and then(mock).should() instead of verify(mock). Pick one style per code base: mixing them makes readers wonder whether they behave differently — they don’t.

Rules that keep mocks honest

Don’t mock what you don’t ownWrap a third-party client (Stripe, S3, an HTTP SDK) in your own small interface and mock that. Test the wrapper against the real thing in an integration test.
Don’t mock valuesRecords, Money, List, LocalDate: just create real ones. Mocking them makes tests longer and hides bugs.
Matchers: all or nothingIf one argument uses a matcher, every argument must: eq("a"), any(), not "a", any() — Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException.
A mock returning a mock is a smellwhen(a.getB().getC()) means the code reaches through objects. Pass what it needs directly.
Verify outcomes, not every callverifyNoMoreInteractions on every test makes harmless refactors fail. Verify the calls that matter.
Too many mocksFive or more mocks in one test means the class has many collaborators. Split it, or test a bigger unit with fakes.

Spies, statics, errors & pitfalls

MockitoFeaturesTest.java✔ 4 / 4 passed
class MockitoFeaturesTest {

  @Test
  void consecutiveAnswersForRetries() {
    PaymentGateway gateway = mock(PaymentGateway.class);
    when(gateway.charge(any(), any()))
      .thenThrow(new PaymentDeclinedException("timeout"))
      .thenReturn("PAY-2");

    Money one = Money.of("1");
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> gateway.charge("a@example.com", one));
    assertThat(gateway.charge("a@example.com", one)).isEqualTo("PAY-2");
    verify(gateway, times(2)).charge(any(), any());
  }

  @Test
  void spyWrapsARealObject() {
    List<String> list = spy(new ArrayList<>());
    list.add("one");
    // on spies use doReturn: when(list.size()) calls the real method
    doReturn(100).when(list).size();

    assertThat(list.size()).isEqualTo(100);
    assertThat(list.get(0)).isEqualTo("one");  // real behaviour kept
    verify(list).add("one");
  }

  @Test
  void mockStaticIsScopedToTheTryBlock() {
    UUID fixed = UUID.fromString("0-0-0-0-42");
    try (MockedStatic<UUID> uuid =
             mockStatic(UUID.class, CALLS_REAL_METHODS)) {
      uuid.when(UUID::randomUUID).thenReturn(fixed);
      assertThat(UUID.randomUUID()).isEqualTo(fixed);
    }
    assertThat(UUID.randomUUID()).isNotEqualTo(fixed); // real again
  }

  @Test
  void finalClassesCanBeMockedByDefault() {
    DiscountPolicy policy = mock(DiscountPolicy.class); // final class
    when(policy.percentFor(any())).thenReturn(50);
    assertThat(policy.percentFor(Money.of("10"))).isEqualTo(50);
  }
}

Clean & maintainable test code requires zero unnecessary code.
Following stubbings are unnecessary (click to navigate to relevant line of code):
1. -> at shop.FailingExamplesTest.d_unnecessaryStubbing(FailingExamplesTest.java:35)
Please remove unnecessary stubbings or use 'lenient' strictness. More info: javadoc for UnnecessaryStubbingException class.

Strictness: MockitoExtension defaults to STRICT_STUBS — unused stubs fail the test. WARN only logs; LENIENT ignores them. Change it with @MockitoSettings(strictness = …) or per stub with lenient().when(…). An unused when(…) is dead setup that misleads readers, so keep the default. The three messages above are real output from deliberately failing tests.

JDK 21+ warningMockito 5’s default inline mock maker (final classes, mockStatic) attaches a Java agent at run time. JDK 21 warns about that; JEP 451 aims to disallow dynamic agent loading by default in a later release. Load Mockito as an agent in the build instead. @{argLine} must already be defined (JaCoCo’s prepare-agent sets it; otherwise declare an empty argLine property).
pom.xml — Mockito as a -javaagent (from Mockito’s docs)
<plugin>  <!-- defines ${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar} -->
  <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>properties</goal></goals></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
<plugin>
  <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
  <configuration>
    <argLine>@{argLine} -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

03 · Test doubles & Mockito

Testing legacy code: characterization tests & seams

Code without tests is hard to change safely, and often hard to test without changing it first. Michael Feathers’ Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004) is a book about that problem; its chapters include “The Seam Model” and “Dependency-Breaking Techniques”. The way out: make the smallest safe change that lets a test in, record what the code does, then improve it.

1 · Find the change pointWhere must the new behaviour go?
2 · Find a test pointWhere can a test observe what that code does — a return value, a file, a call?
3 · Break dependenciesOpen a seam — a place to change behaviour without editing the code there: a constructor parameter, an overridable method.
4 · Pin current behaviourWrite characterization tests: they assert what the code does today, right or wrong.
5 · Change and refactorNow change the code; the tests tell you what else moved.
InvoiceReport.java — the only change: a Clock seam
/**
 * Legacy code, as found — except for ONE change: the Clock.
 * It used to call LocalDate.now() directly, so its output
 * changed every day and no test could pin it down.
 */
public class InvoiceReport {
  private final Clock clock;

  public InvoiceReport() { this(Clock.systemDefaultZone()); }

  public InvoiceReport(Clock clock) {   // the seam
    this.clock = clock;
  }

  /** rows: sku, quantity, unit price */
  public String render(List<String[]> rows) {
    StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
    out.append("INVOICE ").append(LocalDate.now(clock))
       .append('\n');
    double total = 0;
    for (String[] r : rows) {
      int qty = Integer.parseInt(r[1]);
      double price = Double.parseDouble(r[2]);
      double line = qty * price;
      if (qty >= 10) line = line * 0.95;     // bulk discount
      total += line;
      out.append(String.format("%-5s %3d x %7.2f = %8.2f%n",
          r[0], qty, price, line));
    }
    if (total > 1000) total = total - 50;    // ??? nobody knows
    out.append(String.format("TOTAL %.2f%n", total));
    return out.toString();
  }
}
characterization test — a “golden master”5 ✔ · 0.060 s

  @ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} x {1} -> {2}")
  @CsvSource({       // edges found by probing; TODAY's values
      " 9, 100.00, 900.00",     // no bulk discount below 10
      "10, 100.00, 950.00",     // 5% off from 10
      " 1, 1000.00, 1000.00",   // exactly 1000: no 50 off
      " 1, 1000.01, 950.01",    // just above: 50 off
  })
  • Record, don’t judge. “Totals over ₹1,000 lose ₹50” looks like a bug — but someone may rely on it. Pin it, then ask.
  • The seam: LocalDate.now() made the output change daily. A constructor taking a Clock — old callers keep the no-argument one — made it testable without touching the logic.
  • Other seams: subclass and override a method that does I/O; extract an interface for a static call; pass a function instead of calling a singleton.
  • Tools: ApprovalTests automates the received/approved file workflow; Mockito mockStatic (p.16) is a last-resort seam for statics.

Chapter four

Integration & API testing

Unit tests prove each class works alone; integration tests prove they work together — with real HTTP, serialisation, SQL and configuration. They are slower, so keep them focused.

Testing a real HTTP API

OrderApiTest.java
/** Integration test: a real HTTP server on a free port + a real client. */
class OrderApiTest {
  static final OrderRepository repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
  static final OrderApi api = new OrderApi(repo);
  static final HttpClient http = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
  static String baseUrl;

  @BeforeAll static void startServer() throws Exception {
    baseUrl = "http://127.0.0.1:" + api.start();
    repo.save(new Order("ord-1", "asha@example.com",
        List.of(new Item("BOOK", Money.of("600"), 2)),
        Money.of("1140"), Instant.EPOCH));
  }

  @AfterAll static void stopServer() { api.stop(); }

  HttpResponse<String> send(String method, String path)
      throws Exception {
    var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create(baseUrl + path))
        .method(method, HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody()).build();
    return http.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
  }

  @Test void existingOrderReturns200WithJson() throws Exception {
    var res = send("GET", "/orders/ord-1");
    assertThat(res.statusCode()).isEqualTo(200);
    assertThat(res.headers().firstValue("Content-Type"))
      .hasValue("application/json");
    assertThat(res.body())
      .isEqualTo("{\"id\":\"ord-1\",\"total\":\"1140.00\",\"items\":1}");
  }

  @Test void unknownOrderReturns404() throws Exception {
    assertThat(send("GET", "/orders/nope").statusCode()).isEqualTo(404);
  }

  @Test void wrongMethodReturns405WithAllowHeader() throws Exception {
    var res = send("DELETE", "/orders/ord-1");
    assertThat(res.statusCode()).isEqualTo(405);
    assertThat(res.headers().firstValue("Allow")).hasValue("GET");
  }

  // pathTricksAreJustNotFound() → p.36
}
real output4 / 4 passed
OrderApiTest ✔
├─ wrongMethodReturns405WithAllowHeader() ✔
├─ unknownOrderReturns404() ✔
├─ pathTricksAreJustNotFound() ✔
└─ existingOrderReturns200WithJson() ✔
  • Port 0 lets the OS pick a free port, so tests never clash with each other or with a running app.
  • @BeforeAll / @AfterAll start the server once per class — starting it per test would be slow.
  • Check the status, headers and body: a 200 with the wrong Content-Type is still a bug.
  • Test the unhappy paths too: 404 for a missing order, 405 plus an Allow header for a wrong method.
  • JDK HttpServer + HttpClient keep it dependency-free; Spring Boot’s RANDOM_PORT gives the same shape.

Narrow or broad?

Narrow integration test

Exercises one boundary — repository vs real database, client vs stubbed HTTP server.

vs
Broad integration test

Starts most of the application and checks a whole flow through several boundaries.

Prefer many narrow tests: their failures point straight at the broken boundary.
In-memory stand-in

H2 for PostgreSQL, a map for Redis. Fast, but dialects and locking differ.

vs
The real thing in a container

Testcontainers runs production’s PostgreSQL version in Docker.

Fakes for unit tests; the real engine when the database is what you’re testing.

Spring Boot, Testcontainers & contracts

In a Spring Boot application, a test slice starts only the part of the context one layer needs, so it is far faster than @SpringBootTest. Spring Boot 4.0 (November 2025) moved each slice into its own test module.

AnnotationLoadsBoot 4 module

Our first version used static @Container fields per class; that run’s test JVM took 30 s to exit and Failsafe had to kill it. With the container as a Spring bean it closes with the context, and the JVM exited at once.

@MockitoBean, not @MockBeanSpring Framework 6.2 added @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean. Boot 3.4 deprecated @MockBean/@SpyBean, and Boot 4.0 removed them.
@ServiceConnectionSince Boot 3.1: Boot sees the container’s type and wires the connection details for you — no spring.datasource.url juggling.
Testcontainers 2.0October 2025. Module artifacts gained a prefix: testcontainers-postgresql, testcontainers-junit-jupiter.

Calling other services: stubs and contracts

WireMock runs a real HTTP server that returns canned responses, so your client code sends real requests over a socket. Stub the slow, the broken and the odd: timeouts, 500s, malformed JSON, redirects.

The risk: your stub and the real provider drift apart, and both sides stay green while production breaks.

Consumer-driven contract tests (Ian Robinson, 2006) close that gap. The consumer records what it needs from the API; the provider’s build replays those expectations against the real service. Tools: Pact (many languages, a broker to share contracts) and Spring Cloud Contract (JVM, contracts generate stubs and provider tests).

@Transactional in tests: what the rollback hides

@DataJpaTest — and any test class annotated @Transactional — runs each test inside a transaction that is rolled back. That keeps the database clean, but nothing is ever committed, so two kinds of production bug can’t happen in the test. The same code, run both ways against real PostgreSQL:

rolled back · OrderRepositoryIT2 ✔
@DataJpaTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
class OrderRepositoryIT {
  @Autowired OrderRepository repository;

  @Test
  void duplicateReferenceSlipsThroughUntilFlush() {
    repository.save(new CustomerOrder("A-1", BigDecimal.ONE));
    repository.save(new CustomerOrder("A-1", BigDecimal.TWO));
    // no error yet: both INSERTs wait in the session

    assertThatThrownBy(repository::flush)
        .isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class);
  }

  @Test
  void lazyLinesLoadBecauseTheTestHoldsATransaction() {
    repository.saveAndFlush(
        new CustomerOrder("B-1", BigDecimal.TEN)
            .addLine("BOOK", 2).addLine("PEN", 1));

    var order = repository.findByReference("B-1").orElseThrow();
    assertThat(order.getLines()).hasSize(2);   // green here …
  }
}
committed · OrderFlowIT (@SpringBootTest, no @Transactional)3 ✔
  @Autowired OrderRepository repository;

  @BeforeEach
  void cleanSlate() { repository.deleteAll(); } // no rollback

  @Test
  void duplicateReferenceFailsOnSave() {
    repository.save(new CustomerOrder("A-1", BigDecimal.ONE));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> repository.save(
            new CustomerOrder("A-1", BigDecimal.TWO)))
        .isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class);
  }

  @Test
  void lazyLinesFailOutsideATransaction() {
    repository.save(
        new CustomerOrder("B-1", BigDecimal.TEN)
            .addLine("BOOK", 2).addLine("PEN", 1));

    var order = repository.findByReference("B-1").orElseThrow();
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> order.getLines().size()) // red here
        .isInstanceOf(LazyInitializationException.class);
  }

Same code, two outcomes

Inside a rolled-back test transactionCommitted, as in production
Duplicate referencesave() succeeds; the error appears only at flush() — and a test that never flushes stays greensave() commits and throws DataIntegrityViolationException
Lazy lines collectiongetLines() loads, because the test’s transaction is still openLazyInitializationException — the real behaviour with open-in-view=false
Data left behindnone — rolled back after each testrows stay: clean up in @BeforeEach

PostgreSQL’s message in both runs: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_reference_key". Spring translates it to DataIntegrityViolationException. Every test above passes — each one asserts what really happens.

The fix the committed test protects

OrderService.java — map to plain data inside the transaction
  /** Map to a view while the transaction is still open. */
  @Transactional(readOnly = true)
  public Optional<OrderView> find(String reference) {
    return repository.findWithLines(reference).map(OrderView::of);
  }
  • No @Transactional on @SpringBootTest tests. Let each call commit as it would in production; clean up in @BeforeEach.
  • In @DataJpaTest, flush. Testing a constraint or a mapping? Call flush() or saveAndFlush() so the SQL actually runs.
  • Turn off open-in-view (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false) so lazy loading can’t silently happen while JSON is written.
  • Return DTOs, not entities, from transactional services — then no lazy proxy can escape.
  • Keep the fast rolled-back tests; add one committed-path test per repository or flow.
real run · Spring Boot 4.1.1 · GitHub Actions
✔ OrderRepositoryIT  2 tests  11.51 s  (starts PostgreSQL)
✔ OrderFlowIT        3 tests  2.471 s

WARN  org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error : ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_reference_key"
Good to knowRolled-back tests are still the right default for queries, mappings and repository methods — they are fast and leave nothing behind. Call flush() and clear() on the EntityManager (or TestEntityManager) before reading back, so the data really comes from the database.

Database migrations: test them on real data

A migration that works on an empty database can still fail on production’s rows. Run every migration in tests against the same database engine, and for risky ones, against data written by the previous version.

src/main/resources/db/migration — Flyway 13.10
-- V1__create_orders.sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id    text PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL,
  total numeric(12,2) NOT NULL
);

-- V2__add_status.sql
-- new column; existing rows get NULL
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text;

-- V3__status_required.sql
-- backfill first, THEN make it required
UPDATE orders SET status = 'PLACED' WHERE status IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
the draft someone wrote first — no backfill
-- V3__status_required.sql (first draft)
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET NOT NULL;
MigrationsIT — real PostgreSQL 173 ✔ · 5.866 s
  @Test
  void allMigrationsApplyToAnEmptyDatabase() {
    var result = flyway("fresh").load().migrate();

    assertThat(result.migrationsExecuted).isEqualTo(3);
    assertThat(result.targetSchemaVersion).isEqualTo("3");
    flyway("fresh").load().validate();  // checksums unchanged
  }

  @Test
  void v3BackfillsRowsThatAlreadyExist() throws SQLException {
    flyway("live").target("2").load().migrate();   // yesterday
    insertOldOrder("live");

    flyway("live").load().migrate();               // deploy V3

    try (var c = connect(); var rs = c.createStatement()
        .executeQuery("SELECT status FROM live.orders")) {
      rs.next();
      assertThat(rs.getString(1)).isEqualTo("PLACED");
    }
  }

  @Test
  void v3WithoutBackfillFailsOnRealData() throws SQLException {
    flyway("broken").target("2").load().migrate();
    insertOldOrder("broken");

    var withBrokenV3 = flyway("broken")
        .locations("classpath:db/broken")       // only V3
        .ignoreMigrationPatterns("*:missing")   // V1, V2 ran
        .load();

    assertThatThrownBy(withBrokenV3::migrate)
        .isInstanceOf(FlywayException.class)
        .hasMessageContaining("contains null values");
  }
}
  • Empty database: all three migrations apply, and validate() confirms no applied file was edited afterwards.
  • Yesterday’s data: migrate to V2 with target("2"), insert a row as the old app would, then deploy V3. The backfill sets PLACED.
  • The draft without backfill fails on that row, with PostgreSQL’s own error — in CI, not during the release.
  • Let Hibernate validate the schema (spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate) instead of creating it, so entity/column mismatches fail at startup.
  • Never edit an applied migration — add a new one. Flyway’s checksums catch edits.
  • Same idea with Liquibase: update to a tag, insert data, then update again.

Changing a live schema without downtime: expand, then contract

ChangeRelease 1 (expand)Release 2Release 3 (contract)
Make a column requiredadd it nullable; app writes itbackfill old rows, then SET NOT NULL — our V2 → V3—
Rename a columnadd the new column; app writes bothbackfill; app reads the new onedrop the old column
Drop a columnapp stops reading and writing itdrop it—
Index a big tablePostgreSQL CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which can’t run in a transaction: set executeInTransaction=false in the script’s .conf file——

During a rolling deploy the old and the new app run against the same schema, so every step must work with both. Test each step the way MigrationsIT does: migrate to the previous version, write data like the old app, then apply the next step.

Caches: Redis and @Cacheable

A cache is a second copy of the truth. Test what can go wrong: the second call must not reach the source, a change must evict, entries must expire — against a real Redis, where the serializer and the expiry live.

PriceService.java
@Service
public class PriceService {
  private final PriceSource source;

  public PriceService(PriceSource source) {
    this.source = source;
  }

  @Cacheable("prices")
  public Price price(String sku) {
    return source.fetch(sku);
  }

  @CacheEvict("prices")
  public void priceChanged(String sku) {
  }

  /** Calls price() on "this", not the proxy: never cached. */
  public long priceWithTax(String sku) {
    return price(sku).paise() * 118 / 100;
  }

  @Cacheable("quotes")
  public Quote quote(String sku) {
    return new Quote(sku, source.fetch(sku).paise());
  }
}
RedisContainer.java — Redis 8 in Docker
@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class RedisContainer {
  @Bean
  @ServiceConnection(name = "redis")
  GenericContainer<?> redis() {
    return new GenericContainer<>("redis:8-alpine")
        .withExposedPorts(6379);
  }
}

Five cache bugs the tests catch

BugWhat the test showed
Cache never usedtwo calls, fetch() ran once; the key prices::book-1 is in Redis
Stale after a changeafter @CacheEvict the next call fetches again
Self-invocationpriceWithTax() calls price() on this, not on the proxy: fetched twice, nothing in Redis
Value can’t be storedQuote isn’t Serializable: IllegalStateException: Cannot serialize value of type shop.cache.Quote without a serializer — on the first put, at runtime
Never expiresgetExpire() is between 1 and 600 s: time-to-live=10m reached Redis
PriceCacheIT — real Redis4 ✔ · 1.253 s
@SpringBootTest
@Import(RedisContainer.class)
class PriceCacheIT {
  @Autowired PriceService prices;
  @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redis;
  @MockitoSpyBean PriceSource source;

  @BeforeEach
  void emptyCache() {
    redis.delete(redis.keys("*"));
    clearInvocations(source);
  }

  @Test
  void secondCallIsServedFromRedis() {
    prices.price("book-1");
    assertThat(redis.hasKey("prices::book-1")).isTrue();
    prices.price("book-1");

    verify(source, times(1)).fetch("book-1");
    assertThat(redis.hasKey("prices::book-1")).isTrue();
    assertThat(redis.getExpire("prices::book-1"))
        .isBetween(1L, 600L);              // TTL 10m applied
  }

  @Test
  void evictingMakesTheNextCallFetchAgain() {
    prices.price("book-1");
    prices.priceChanged("book-1");
    prices.price("book-1");

    verify(source, times(2)).fetch("book-1");
  }

  @Test
  void selfInvocationBypassesTheCache() {
    prices.priceWithTax("book-1");
    prices.priceWithTax("book-1");

    verify(source, times(2)).fetch("book-1");
    assertThat(redis.hasKey("prices::book-1")).isFalse();
  }

  @Test
  void aValueThatIsNotSerializableFailsOnlyAtRuntime() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> prices.quote("book-1"))
        .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class)
        .hasMessage("Cannot serialize value of type "
            + "shop.cache.Quote without a serializer");
  }
}
Rule of thumbTests that are not about caching set spring.cache.type=none, so they can’t pass by reading a value an earlier test left behind.
Good to knowOur two Redis test classes use different Spring configurations, so each got its own context — and its own container (started in 0.2 s and 0.2 s). Same configuration, one context, one container.

A flaky cache test: Redis writes are asynchronous

Our first PriceCacheIT failed now and then. Repeated in CI it failed 6 times in 30 runs: sometimes the value was not in Redis right after price() returned; sometimes the call after @CacheEvict still got the old value. It was not a test bug. Since Spring Data Redis 4.0, with Lettuce, put, evict and clear are asynchronous: they “may complete after the calling method returns”.

AsyncCacheWritesIT — the default, measured1 ✔ · 2.234 s
/** The library default, no immediate writes: count the lag. */
@SpringBootTest(properties =
    "shop.cache.immediate-writes=false")
@Import(RedisContainer.class)
class AsyncCacheWritesIT {
  @Autowired PriceService prices;
  @Autowired StringRedisTemplate redis;

  @Test
  void writesLandAfterTheCallReturns() {
    int notYet = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
      prices.price("sku-" + i);
      if (!redis.hasKey("prices::sku-" + i)) {
        notYet++;
      }
    }
    System.out.println("[async writes] " + notYet + " of 1000"
        + " entries were not in Redis when price() returned");

    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).until(
        () -> redis.keys("prices::sku-*").size() == 1000);
  }
}
real output · CI
[async writes] 303 of 1000 entries were not in Redis when price() returned
CacheConfig.java — the fix: wait for writes
/**
 * Spring Data Redis 4 with Lettuce: put() and evict() are
 * asynchronous by default and can finish after the call
 * returns. Wait for them: a read right after a write must
 * see it.
 */
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class CacheConfig {
  @Bean
  @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "shop.cache.immediate-writes",
      havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
  RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer immediateWrites(
      RedisConnectionFactory redis) {
    return builder -> builder.cacheWriter(RedisCacheWriter
        .create(redis, w -> w.immediateWrites()));
  }
}

What the failing runs reported

TestWhat it sawWhy
secondCallIsServedFromRedisright after price() the key was not in Redis: Expecting value to be true but was falsethe SET was still on its way
evictingMakesTheNextCallFetchAgainafter priceChanged() the next call still got the cached value: Wanted 2 times … But was 1 timethe DEL was still on its way

Source: Spring Data Redis reference, “Migration Guides”, 3.x → 4.x: the default RedisCacheWriter is asynchronous for put, evict and clear when the connection factory is also a ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory — which Lettuce’s is. There is no Spring Boot property for it; the customizer above is the switch.

How we found it: repeat the test

flake-hunt.yml — run from the Actions tab
for i in $(seq "$RUNS"); do
  if ! mvn -B -ntp verify -Dit.test="$TEST" -Dtest=NoUnit \
    -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false > run.log 2>&1; then
    fails=$((fails+1))
    echo "::warning title=run $i failed::$msg"
  fi
done

Three machines, ten runs each: 3, 2 and 1 failures before the fix; 0, 0 and 0 after it.

  • A flaky test is a bug report — about the test or about the code. Find out which before you add a retry.
  • Measure the window: 303 of 1000 writes had not landed when the method returned. The same race exists in production: an evicted price can be served once more.
  • Decide on purpose. Need read-your-writes (evict on change, then read)? Use immediateWrites(). Prefer throughput? Keep the default and let tests wait with Awaitility, as AsyncCacheWritesIT does.
  • Cache.evictIfPresent(…) and invalidate(…) always wait, whatever the setting.
  • A retry would have hidden it. Surefire’s rerunFailingTestsCount turns this into a “flaky pass” — and the production race stays.
  • With the fix, the strict test stayed green in 30 of 30 repeated runs.

Scheduled jobs: the rule and the wiring

A scheduled job is two things: a rule (which carts are abandoned?) and wiring (does it really run every ten minutes?). Test the rule as a plain method with a fixed clock — fast, exact, every boundary. Test the wiring once, with the schedule shortened and Awaitility waiting for the effect.

CartCleanup.java
@Component
public class CartCleanup {
  static final Duration MAX_AGE = Duration.ofHours(24);
  private final CartStore carts;
  private final Clock clock;

  public CartCleanup(CartStore carts, Clock clock) {
    this.carts = carts;
    this.clock = clock;
  }

  /** The schedule is wiring; the rule is a plain method. */
  @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${shop.cleanup.every:PT10M}")
  public void scheduledRun() {
    removeAbandoned();
  }

  public int removeAbandoned() {
    var cutoff = clock.instant().minus(MAX_AGE);
    return carts.removeTouchedBefore(cutoff);
  }
}
CartCleanupTest — unit, fixed clock2 ✔ · 0.018 s
/** The rule, without Spring or a scheduler: plain and fast. */
class CartCleanupTest {
  Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-10-13T10:00:00Z");
  CartStore carts = new CartStore();
  CartCleanup cleanup = new CartCleanup(carts,
      Clock.fixed(now, ZoneOffset.UTC));

  @Test
  void removesCartsUntouchedForMoreThan24Hours() {
    carts.touch("old", now.minus(Duration.ofHours(25)));
    carts.touch("fresh", now.minus(Duration.ofHours(1)));

    assertThat(cleanup.removeAbandoned()).isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(carts.ids()).containsExactly("fresh");
  }

  @Test
  void exactly24HoursOldIsKept() {
    carts.touch("edge", now.minus(Duration.ofHours(24)));

    assertThat(cleanup.removeAbandoned()).isZero();
  }
}
CartCleanupScheduleIT — real scheduler1 ✔ · 0.942 s
/** The wiring: the schedule really fires (here every 0.2 s). */
@SpringBootTest(properties = {"shop.cleanup.every=PT0.2S",
    "spring.cache.type=none"})
class CartCleanupScheduleIT {
  @Autowired CartStore carts;

  @Test
  void theScheduledRunRemovesAbandonedCarts() {
    carts.touch("abandoned", Instant.EPOCH);

    await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .until(() -> carts.ids().isEmpty());
  }
}
NightlyReport.java — a cron schedule
/** 02:00 on weekdays, India time, whatever the server's zone. */
public static final String CRON = "0 0 2 * * MON-FRI";
public static final String ZONE = "Asia/Kolkata";
private final AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger();

@Scheduled(cron = CRON, zone = ZONE)
NightlyReportCronTest2 ✔ · 0.013 s
/** A cron expression is code: test when it fires. */
class NightlyReportCronTest {
  CronExpression cron = CronExpression.parse(NightlyReport.CRON);

  @Test
  void fridayNightRunsNextOnMondayAt2() {
    var friday = LocalDateTime.parse("2026-10-16T22:00");
    assertThat(cron.next(friday))
        .isEqualTo(LocalDateTime.parse("2026-10-19T02:00"));
  }

  @Test
  void exactly2amRunsTheNextWeekdayNotAgain() {
    var tuesday2am = LocalDateTime.parse("2026-10-13T02:00");
    assertThat(cron.next(tuesday2am))
        .isEqualTo(LocalDateTime.parse("2026-10-14T02:00"));
  }
}
  • Inject a Clock, never call Instant.now(): the unit test pins time and tests “exactly 24 hours” both ways.
  • Keep the rule a plain public method. The @Scheduled method only calls it, so the rule needs no Spring.
  • The schedule is a property (${shop.cleanup.every:PT10M}), so one test can run it every 0.2 s.
  • A cron expression is code. CronExpression.parse(…).next(…) answers “when next?” without waiting; pin the zone.
  • Wait for the effect with await().atMost(…); never Thread.sleep and hope.
  • A fixedDelay job also runs once as soon as the context starts — in every @SpringBootTest. If it changes shared data, put it behind @ConditionalOnProperty and switch it off in tests.

Batch jobs: Spring Batch 6

A batch job reads, processes and writes in chunks, and must decide what to do with bad records. Test the processor as plain Java; test the whole job with @SpringBatchTest on a small file in which every line has a purpose — then the counts prove the job did the right thing with each one.

ImportPricesJob.java — the step
@Bean
Step importStep(JobRepository repo, PriceCatalog catalog,
    FlatFileItemReader<PriceLine> reader) {
  return new StepBuilder("importStep", repo)
      .<PriceLine, Price>chunk(100)
      .reader(reader)
      .processor(new ToPaise())
      .writer(chunk -> chunk.forEach(catalog::put))
      .faultTolerant()
      .skip(FlatFileParseException.class)
      .skipLimit(5)
      .build();
}
ToPaise.java — the processor
/** Rupees to paise; a negative price is filtered (null). */
public class ToPaise
    implements ItemProcessor<PriceLine, Price> {
  @Override
  public Price process(PriceLine line) {
    if (line.rupees().signum() < 0) {
      return null;
    }
    BigDecimal paise = line.rupees().movePointRight(2);
    return new Price(line.sku(), paise.longValueExact());
  }
}
ImportPricesJobIT — the whole job1 ✔ · 0.539 s
/** prices.csv: 3 good lines, 1 negative, 1 broken. */
@SpringBootTest(properties = "spring.cache.type=none")
@SpringBatchTest
class ImportPricesJobIT {
  @Autowired JobOperatorTestUtils jobs;
  @Autowired PriceCatalog catalog;

  @Test
  void filtersNegativeAndSkipsBrokenLines() throws Exception {
    JobExecution run = jobs.startJob();

    assertThat(run.getStatus())
        .isEqualTo(BatchStatus.COMPLETED);
    StepExecution step =
        run.getStepExecutions().iterator().next();
    assertThat(step.getReadCount()).isEqualTo(4);
    assertThat(step.getFilterCount()).isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(step.getReadSkipCount()).isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(step.getWriteCount()).isEqualTo(3);
    assertThat(catalog.get("book-2"))
        .contains(new Price("book-2", 129_950));
  }
}

  • The job completed: read 4, filtered 1, skipped 1, wrote 3 — the step ran in 21 ms in CI.
  • JobOperatorTestUtils (Batch 6; formerly JobLauncherTestUtils) starts the job with unique parameters, so it can run again.
  • spring.batch.job.enabled=false: Boot otherwise runs the job when the application starts.
  • No database needed: with spring-boot-starter-batch the job repository is in memory; spring-boot-starter-batch-jdbc stores it in tables.
  • Batch 6 builds a step with chunk(100); the transaction manager is optional (the chunk(int, PlatformTransactionManager) form is deprecated).
  • Also test the skip limit: one more bad line than allowed must fail the job, not import half a file.

Messaging & async: Kafka with Testcontainers

Kafka (like most brokers) delivers at least once: after a consumer crash or rebalance, a message can arrive again. So the test that matters is not “can I send and receive” but “does a duplicate do any harm?”. A real broker in a container answers that.

OrderEventConsumer.java — idempotent by event id
/**
 * Kafka delivers at least once: an event can arrive twice.
 * This consumer is idempotent - each event id is applied once.
 */
public class OrderEventConsumer implements AutoCloseable {
  private final KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer;
  private final Set<String> applied =
      ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
  private final AtomicInteger received = new AtomicInteger();
  private final Thread loop;

  public OrderEventConsumer(String servers, String topic) {
    consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(Map.of(
        ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, servers,
        ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "order-projection",
        ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest"),
        new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer());
    consumer.subscribe(List.of(topic));
    loop = Thread.ofPlatform().name("order-events")
        .start(this::run);
  }

  private void run() {
    try {
      while (true) {
        var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200));
        for (var record : records) {
          received.incrementAndGet();
          var id = record.headers().lastHeader("event-id");
          applied.add(new String(id.value(), UTF_8));
          // adding an id that is already there changes nothing
        }
      }
    } catch (WakeupException stopping) {
      // close() was called
    } finally {
      consumer.close();
    }
  }

  public int received() { return received.get(); }
  public int applied() { return applied.size(); }

  @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException {
    consumer.wakeup();
    loop.join();
  }
}
OrderEventsIT — real Kafka 4.3.1 broker1 ✔ · 3.961 s
class OrderEventsIT {
  static final KafkaContainer KAFKA =
      new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka-native:4.3.1");
  static { KAFKA.start(); }      // singleton per test JVM

  @Test
  void redeliveredEventIsAppliedOnlyOnce() throws Exception {
    String kafka = KAFKA.getBootstrapServers();
    String paid = "{\"status\":\"PAID\"}";
    try (var out = new OrderEventPublisher(kafka, "orders");
         var in = new OrderEventConsumer(kafka, "orders")) {

      out.publish("evt-1", "ord-1", paid);
      out.publish("evt-1", "ord-1", paid);    // redelivered
      out.publish("evt-2", "ord-2", paid);

      await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(30))  // no sleep
          .untilAsserted(() -> {
            assertThat(in.received()).isEqualTo(3);
            assertThat(in.applied()).isEqualTo(2);
          });
    }
  }
}
OrderEventPublisher.java (excerpt)
  public void publish(String eventId, String orderId,
      String json)
      throws Exception {
    var record = new ProducerRecord<>(topic, orderId, json);
    record.headers().add("event-id",
        eventId.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    producer.send(record).get();      // wait for the broker ack
  }
  • Real run: the apache/kafka-native container started in 0.5 s; three messages arrived, two were applied.
  • Wait, don’t sleep. Awaitility polls until the assertion holds or the timeout expires — fast when things work, a clear failure when they don’t.
  • Isolate tests: a unique topic or consumer group per test, so leftovers from one test can’t satisfy another.
  • Test the unhappy paths: a poison message, a consumer that crashes mid-batch, a redelivery after restart.

E-mail: testing with GreenMail

Customers notice e-mails more than most features: a wrong total, a missing confirmation, a mail sent twice. GreenMail (Apache-2.0) runs a real SMTP server inside the test JVM, so your code sends real mail over a real socket — and the test reads it back.

OrderMailer.java — plain Jakarta Mail (Angus Mail 2.0.5)
/** Sends order e-mails through any SMTP server. */
public class OrderMailer {
  private final Session session;

  public OrderMailer(String host, int port) {
    Properties props = new Properties();
    props.put("mail.smtp.host", host);
    props.put("mail.smtp.port", String.valueOf(port));
    props.put("mail.smtp.connectiontimeout", "2000");
    session = Session.getInstance(props);
  }

  public void sendConfirmation(String to, String orderId,
      String total) throws MessagingException {
    var message = new MimeMessage(session);
    message.setFrom(new InternetAddress("orders@shop.example"));
    message.setRecipients(Message.RecipientType.TO, to);
    message.setSubject("Order " + orderId + " confirmed",
        "UTF-8");
    message.setText("Thank you! Total: " + total, "UTF-8");
    Transport.send(message);
  }
}
OrderMailerTest — GreenMail JUnit 5 extension2 ✔ · 0.158 s
/** GreenMail: a real SMTP server inside the test JVM. */
class OrderMailerTest {
  @RegisterExtension                  // fresh mailbox per test
  static GreenMailExtension smtp = new GreenMailExtension(
      ServerSetupTest.SMTP.dynamicPort());   // any free port

  OrderMailer mailer() {
    int port = smtp.getSmtp().getPort();
    return new OrderMailer("localhost", port);
  }

  @Test
  void confirmationIsSentToTheCustomer() throws Exception {
    mailer().sendConfirmation("asha@example.com", "ord-1",
        "₹1,140.00");

    assertThat(smtp.waitForIncomingEmail(2_000, 1)).isTrue();
    MimeMessage mail = smtp.getReceivedMessages()[0];
    assertThat(mail.getSubject())
        .isEqualTo("Order ord-1 confirmed");
    assertThat(mail.getAllRecipients())
        .extracting(Object::toString)
        .containsExactly("asha@example.com");
    assertThat((String) mail.getContent())
        .isEqualTo("Thank you! Total: ₹1,140.00");
  }

  @Test
  void smtpServerDownIsAnError() {
    var nobodyListening = new OrderMailer("localhost", 1);

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> nobodyListening.sendConfirmation(
            "asha@example.com", "ord-2", "₹10.00"))
        .isInstanceOf(MessagingException.class);
  }
}
Check in every e-mail testWhy
Recipient and sendera wrong address is a privacy incident
Subject and body textorder number, total, links — what the customer reads
Encodingthe ₹ sign survived here because subject and body are sent as UTF-8
Failure pathserver down or rejected: retry, queue, or tell the user

Four ways to test e-mail

OptionWhat it isUse for
Mock the portMockito mock of your EmailSender interface (p.14)unit tests: was an e-mail requested?
GreenMail in-processgreenmail-junit5 2.1.14: real SMTP, IMAP, POP3 inside the test JVMthe default: real SMTP, no Docker
GreenMail in a containerthe greenmail/standalone imagenon-Java services, shared test environments
MailpitSMTP server with a web UI and REST API, in a containerend-to-end and manual checks of real HTML mails
  • Assert what the customer sees: recipient, subject, body — and that the server being down is an error you handle, not a lost mail.
  • Free ports: ServerSetupTest.SMTP is a fixed port (3025); .dynamicPort() picks a free one, so parallel forks never clash.
  • Spring Boot: point spring.mail.host and spring.mail.port at GreenMail with @DynamicPropertySource; JavaMailSender needs no change.
  • Never let tests reach a real mail server: one wrong address and a customer gets a test mail.

Cloud services: AWS and Azure emulators

Code that talks to S3, SQS or Azure Storage can be tested against emulators in containers: the real SDK, real HTTP, no cloud account and no bill. One abstract test class runs the same checks against every AWS emulator; Azure gets the same two tests.

AwsStorageContract — AWS SDK v2 (excerpt)
  @Test
  void storesAndReadsAnInvoice() {
    try (var s3 = s3()) {
      s3.createBucket(b -> b.bucket("invoices"));
      s3.putObject(b -> b.bucket("invoices").key("ord-1.txt"),
          RequestBody.fromString("TOTAL 1768.74"));

      String text = s3.getObjectAsBytes(b -> b
          .bucket("invoices").key("ord-1.txt")).asUtf8String();
      assertThat(text).isEqualTo("TOTAL 1768.74");
    }
  }

  @Test
  void queuesAndReceivesAMessage() {
    try (var sqs = sqs()) {
      String url = sqs.createQueue(b -> b.queueName("orders"))
          .queueUrl();
      sqs.sendMessage(b -> b.queueUrl(url)
          .messageBody("ord-1 PAID"));

      var messages = sqs.receiveMessage(
          b -> b.queueUrl(url).waitTimeSeconds(5)).messages();
      assertThat(messages).extracting(Message::body)
          .containsExactly("ord-1 PAID");
    }
  }
  // queuesAndReceivesAMessage(): SQS create / send / receive
}
