3 · fetching a real token over HTTP
  /** client_credentials grant against the mock server. */
  String token(String issuerId, String scope) {
    var form = new LinkedMultiValueMap<String, String>();
    form.add("grant_type", "client_credentials");
    form.add("client_id", "reporting-job");
    form.add("client_secret", "any");
    form.add("scope", scope);
    Map<?, ?> body = http.post()
        .uri(issuer(issuerId) + "/token")
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED)
        .body(form).retrieve().body(Map.class);
    return (String) body.get("access_token");
  }

Calling other services: WireMock & retries

Your code will meet slow, failing and strange responses from the services it calls. WireMock (Apache-2.0) is a real HTTP server you script per test, so you can produce those failures on demand — and prove your timeouts and retries (here Resilience4j) behave.

PriceClient.java — timeout, error mapping (excerpt)
  public BigDecimal priceOf(String sku) {
    return retry.executeSupplier(() -> fetch(sku));
  }

  private BigDecimal fetch(String sku) {
    var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(
            baseUrl.resolve("/prices/" + sku))
        .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))  // never wait forever
        .build();
    HttpResponse<String> response;
    try {
      response = http.send(request,
          HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
    } catch (IOException e) {             // timeouts included
      throw new UpstreamException("unreachable", e);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
      Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
      throw new IllegalStateException(e);
    }
    int status = response.statusCode();
    if (status == 404) throw new NoSuchElementException(sku);
    if (status >= 500) {
      throw new UpstreamException("HTTP " + status, null);
    }
    var m = PRICE.matcher(response.body());
    if (!m.find()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("bad price JSON: "
          + response.body());
    }
    return new BigDecimal(m.group(1));
  }
}
Retries.java — Resilience4j 2.4.0
  /** 3 attempts, 100 ms apart, only for retryable failures. */
  public static Retry forPrices() {
    return Retry.of("prices", RetryConfig.custom()
        .maxAttempts(3)
        .waitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(100))
        .retryExceptions(UpstreamException.class)
        .build());
  }
PriceClientTest — WireMock 3.13.25 ✔ · 3.421 s
/** WireMock: a real HTTP server that answers as told. */
class PriceClientTest {
  @RegisterExtension
  static WireMockExtension wm = WireMockExtension.newInstance()
      .options(wireMockConfig().dynamicPort()).build();

  static final String PATH = "/prices/BOOK";
  static final String BOOK = """
      {"sku":"BOOK","price":"600.00"}""";

  PriceClient client = new PriceClient(
      URI.create(wm.baseUrl()), Retries.forPrices());

  @Test
  void returnsThePrice() {
    wm.stubFor(get(PATH).willReturn(okJson(BOOK)));

    assertThat(client.priceOf("BOOK")).isEqualTo("600.00");
  }

  @Test
  void twoOutagesThenSuccessIsRetried() {
    wm.stubFor(get(PATH).inScenario("flaky")
        .whenScenarioStateIs(STARTED)
        .willReturn(serviceUnavailable()).willSetStateTo("2"));
    wm.stubFor(get(PATH).inScenario("flaky")
        .whenScenarioStateIs("2")
        .willReturn(serverError()).willSetStateTo("up"));
    wm.stubFor(get(PATH).inScenario("flaky")
        .whenScenarioStateIs("up").willReturn(okJson(BOOK)));

    assertThat(client.priceOf("BOOK")).isEqualTo("600.00");
    wm.verify(3, getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo(PATH)));
  }

  @Test
  void slowServiceTimesOutAfterThreeTries() {
    wm.stubFor(get(PATH)
        .willReturn(okJson(BOOK).withFixedDelay(2_000)));

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.priceOf("BOOK"))
        .isInstanceOf(UpstreamException.class)
        .hasMessage("unreachable");
    wm.verify(3, getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo(PATH)));
  }

  // … unknownProductIsNotRetried, malformedJsonIsAClearError
}

What each stub proves

StubExpected behaviourChecked with
503, then 500, then 200 (a scenario)two retries, then the priceverify(3, getRequestedFor(…))
200 after a 2-second delay500 ms timeout, three attempts, then UpstreamExceptionwithFixedDelay(2_000), 3 requests
404no retry — retrying can’t make a missing product appearexactly 1 request
HTML instead of JSONa clear error naming the bad bodyhasMessageStartingWith
  • Retry only what can succeed next time: timeouts and 5xx yes; 4xx and bad data no.
  • Always set a timeout. Java’s HttpClient waits forever by default; one slow service then ties up every thread.
  • Verify the number of calls, not just the result — a retry loop that silently fires 50 times is a bug too.
  • Stubs drift from the real service; pair them with a contract test (p.31).

Contract testing with Pact

A WireMock stub says what you think the other service returns. A consumer-driven contract makes that belief checkable: the consumer’s test records what it needs, and the provider’s build replays it against the real API. Break the contract and the provider’s build goes red — before anything ships.

consumer test1 ✔ · 0.882 s
@ExtendWith(PactConsumerTestExt.class)
@PactTestFor(providerName = "orders")
class OrderStatusConsumerPactTest {

  @Pact(consumer = "shop", provider = "orders")
  V4Pact paidOrder(PactDslWithProvider builder) {
    return builder
        .given("order ord-1 is paid")
        .uponReceiving("a status request for ord-1")
          .path("/orders/ord-1/status").method("GET")
        .willRespondWith()
          .status(200)
          .body(new PactDslJsonBody()
              .stringValue("id", "ord-1")
              .stringType("status", "PAID"))   // any string
        .toPact(V4Pact.class);
  }

  @Test
  void readsTheStatus(MockServer server) throws Exception {
    var client =
        new OrderStatusClient(URI.create(server.getUrl()));

    assertThat(client.statusOf("ord-1")).isEqualTo("PAID");
  }
}

  • Spring Cloud Contract works the other way round: the provider writes the contract and publishes stubs for consumers.

Time, randomness, threads & flaky tests

A test that passes and fails without any code change is flaky. Flaky tests are worse than none: people learn to press “re-run”, and real failures get ignored. Almost every cause is something the test doesn’t control.

TrickyThingsTest.java
class TrickyThingsTest {

  @Test void timeComesFromAnInjectedClock() {
    Instant newYearsEve = Instant.parse("2026-12-31T23:59:59Z");
    Clock clock = Clock.fixed(newYearsEve, ZoneOffset.UTC);
    var service = new OrderService(new InMemoryOrderRepository(),
        (c, m) -> "PAY", (to, s, b) -> {}, new DiscountPolicy(), clock);

    Order o = service.placeOrder("a@example.com",
        List.of(new Item("PEN", Money.of("1"), 1)));

    assertThat(o.placedAt()).isEqualTo(newYearsEve);
  }

  @Test void randomnessComesFromASeed() {
    var a = new Random(42).ints(5, 0, 100).boxed().toList();
    var b = new Random(42).ints(5, 0, 100).boxed().toList();
    assertThat(a).isEqualTo(b);  // same seed, same sequence
  }

  @Test void filesGoInAFreshTempDir(@TempDir Path dir) throws Exception {
    Path report = dir.resolve("report.csv");
    Files.writeString(report, "sku,qty\nPEN,2\n");
    assertThat(Files.readAllLines(report))
        .containsExactly("sku,qty", "PEN,2");
  }  // JUnit deletes dir afterwards

  @Test void concurrentSavesAreAllKept() throws Exception {
    var repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    int threads = 16, perThread = 500;
    var start = new CountDownLatch(1);
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) {
      for (int t = 0; t < threads; t++) {
        int base = t * perThread;
        pool.submit(() -> {
          start.await();  // release all threads at once
          for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++)
            repo.save(new Order("o" + (base + i), "x@example.com",
                List.of(), Money.of("0"), Instant.EPOCH));
          return null;
        });
      }
      start.countDown();
    }  // close() waits for all tasks
    for (int i = 0; i < threads * perThread; i++)
      assertThat(repo.findById("o" + i)).isPresent();
  }

  @Test void slowCodeFailsFastInsteadOfHangingTheBuild() {
    assertTimeoutPreemptively(Duration.ofSeconds(1),
        () -> new DiscountPolicy().percentFor(Money.of("1")));
  }
}

Where flakiness comes from

CauseFix
Real time
LocalDate.now() breaks at midnight, month end, DST
Inject a Clock; use Clock.fixed
Randomness
UUIDs, shuffles, random test data
Seed it, or inject the generator
Sleeping
Thread.sleep(500) is too short on a busy CI box
Wait for a condition (Awaitility) with a timeout
Shared state
Static fields, a shared DB row, a singleton cache
Fresh fixtures per test; unique IDs; reset in @AfterEach
Test order
Test B only passes after test A
Each test sets up its own data; run in random order to find these
Time zone / locale
Passes in Bengaluru, fails on a UTC build agent
Set zone and locale explicitly in code and tests
Network
Calls to real external services
Stub at the boundary; containers for owned dependencies
Concurrency
Races appear one run in a hundred
Latches to line threads up; repeat; stress in a separate job
  • Clock.fixed makes “now” a constant; production passes Clock.systemUTC().
  • new Random(42) gives the same sequence on every run and every machine.
  • @TempDir — no leftovers between runs, no clashes between parallel tests.
  • CountDownLatch releases 16 threads together so they really overlap: 8,000 concurrent saves, none lost.
  • assertTimeoutPreemptively stops a hung test instead of hanging the whole build.
  • For async code, poll for a condition with Awaitility (await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(…)) instead of sleeping.
Rule of thumbTreat a flaky test like a bug. Quarantine it (a separate, non-blocking job), open a ticket, and fix or delete it within days — never add an automatic “retry until green” to the main build.

04 · Integration & API testing

Concurrency bugs: jcstress

count++ looks like one step; it is three — read, add, write. Two threads can both read 0 and both write 1. An ordinary test almost never sees it: the window is nanoseconds. jcstress (OpenJDK) runs a tiny test hundreds of millions of times, with the interpreter, C1 and C2 and compiler stress modes, and counts every outcome.

RacyCounterTest.java
/** Two threads each do count++ once. Is the result always 2? */
@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "both counted")
@Outcome(id = "1", expect = ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING,
    desc = "lost update: count++ is read, add, write")
@State
public class RacyCounterTest {
  int count;

  @Actor
  public void first() {
    count++;
  }

  @Actor
  public void second() {
    count++;
  }

  @Arbiter
  public void result(I_Result r) {
    r.r1 = count;
  }
}
AtomicCounterTest.java
/** The fix. A lost update would now fail the run. */
@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "both counted")
@Outcome(id = "1", expect = FORBIDDEN, desc = "lost update")
@State
public class AtomicCounterTest {
  final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();

  @Actor
  public void first() {
    count.incrementAndGet();
  }

  @Actor
  public void second() {
    count.incrementAndGet();
  }

  @Arbiter
  public void result(I_Result r) {
    r.r1 = count.get();
  }
}

       1  200,651,963   18.00%  Interesting  lost update: count++ is read, add, write
       2  914,222,425   82.00%   Acceptable  both counted

AtomicCounterTest — results across all configurations

Actor 1Actor 2ForksLost
InterpreterInterpreter20.99–11.67%
InterpreterC120.24–2.80%

  • 200,651,963 lost updates in 1,114,874,388 runs (18.00%). The rate depended on how each actor was compiled: from 0.14% to 67.08%.
  • ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING reports an outcome but passes; FORBIDDEN fails the run — so the atomic version guards the fix.
  • Use it for code that shares memory without locks: custom counters and caches, lazy initialisation, publishing objects to other threads.
  • Ordinary code: avoid shared mutable state, use java.util.concurrent.
  • Run -m quick in CI; default or tough before a release. Tests live in src/main, by jcstress convention.

Beyond correctness

Passing unit and integration tests prove the parts are right. This chapter checks the whole system from the outside: real browsers clicking real pages, real load on real servers, and an attacker’s view of your code.

Choosing locators (Playwright’s order)

1
Role + name · getByRole(BUTTON, name "Checkout") — what users and screen readers see
2
Text · getByText("Order confirmed") — user-visible, but changes with copy
3
Label / placeholder · getByLabel("Email") for form fields
4
Test id · getByTestId reads data-testid by default — stable, invisible to users
5
CSS / XPath · div.cart > span:nth-child(3) — last resort; breaks on any layout change

Real run on GitHub Actions: Playwright for Java 1.63.0 drove Chromium against a small shop page; both journeys passed, and each test saved a screenshot and a trace (target/*-trace.zip, open with playwright show-trace). The total appears 300 ms after checkout — the assertion waited for it, no sleep.

Page ObjectsWrap each page in a class with intent-revealing methods. When the HTML changes, you fix one class, not fifty tests.
Never sleepWait for a condition, not a duration. Playwright’s locators and web-first assertions retry automatically until a timeout.
Keep them fewCover the journeys that make money or lose data — sign-up, checkout, payment — plus a few read-only smoke tests in production after each deploy.
Own your dataCreate users and products through the API at the start of each test; don’t depend on what is already in the environment.
AccessibilityRun axe-core (Deque publishes Java bindings for Selenium and Playwright) on key pages; it flags missing labels and poor contrast automatically.
Traces, not guessesKeep Playwright traces and screenshots as CI artefacts. Comparing screenshots also catches visual regressions — mask dates and other changing areas.

05 · Beyond correctness

Performance testing

Kinds of performance test

LoadExpected peak traffic, held steadyDoes it meet the latency target at normal peak?
StressRamp beyond the peak until it breaksWhere is the limit, and does it fail gracefully?
SpikeA sudden jump: 10× in secondsDo autoscaling, queues and pools cope?
SoakNormal load for hoursMemory leaks, connection leaks, growing queues
ScalabilityRepeat with 1, 2, 4 instancesDoes capacity grow with hardware?

Tools

GatlingJava, Kotlin or Scala DSL; load tests as code; HTML reports3.16
Apache JMeterGUI to build test plans, CLI to run them; many protocols5.6.3
Grafana k6Tests in JavaScript; single binary; good CI fit2.3
JMHMicrobenchmarks for one method; handles JIT warm-up and dead-code elimination1.37
Rule of thumbReport percentiles, not averages. p99 = 99% of requests were at least this fast. A page that makes 100 calls has a 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 63% chance that at least one of them is slower than p99.

A real load test — and what it found

LoadSmoke.java — virtual users against OrderApi
try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  for (int u = 0; u < users; u++) {
    pool.submit(() -> {
      while (System.nanoTime() < end) {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try {
          var res = http.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
          if (res.statusCode() != 200) errors.inc();
        } catch (Exception e) { errors.inc(); }
        if (t0 > warmUpEnd) latencies.add(System.nanoTime() - t0);
      }
      return null;
    });
  }
}

users=50  requests=12,150  errors=0  throughput=1,215 req/s

Run (10 s measured, after 3 s warm-up)req/sp50 msp95 msp99 msmax msmean ms
1 user2441.9942.0942.2643.9642.01
10 users24441.0041.1242.0244.1341.04
50 users1,21541.0042.0043.0458.4441.15
1 user · TCP_NODELAY4,7210.190.310.357.560.21
50 users · TCP_NODELAY13,9973.097.6610.7121.383.57

The finding. Every request took about 42 ms — even with a single user, so it wasn’t load. Our handler sends the headers and the body as two separate small writes; with Nagle’s algorithm on, the second waits for the client’s delayed ACK — the Nagle/delayed-ACK stall (the companion book’s chapter 1 measures it packet by packet). Starting the JVM with -Dsun.net.httpserver.nodelay=true (sets TCP_NODELAY) cut the single-user p50 from 42 ms to 0.19 ms. No unit test could have found this. The companion book, Java Performance Deep Dives, takes this stall apart packet by packet.

Little’s Law checks your numbers: users in flight = throughput × time in system. 50 users ÷ 1,215 req/s = 41.2 ms (measured mean 41.1 ms), and 50 ÷ 13,997 = 3.6 ms (measured 3.6 ms). If your tool’s numbers don’t satisfy it, the load generator itself is the bottleneck. These figures come from this guide’s 2-CPU sandbox: compare runs, not absolute numbers.

Watch outCoordinated omission: a closed-loop tool like this one stops sending while the server stalls, so slow periods produce fewer samples and percentiles look better than reality. Open-model tools (Gatling’s constantUsersPerSec, k6 arrival-rate executors) keep sending at a fixed rate.

05 · Beyond correctness

Security & resilience testing

Security testing is mostly automation you add to the pipeline once, plus security cases you write like any other test. The scanners find known problems; your own tests prove your rules — who may see what — actually hold.

KindWhat it doesJava-friendly toolsWhen
SASTReads source or bytecode for dangerous patternsSpotBugs + Find Security Bugs, Semgrep, CodeQLEvery build
SCAFinds libraries with known vulnerabilities (CVEs)OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot, RenovateEvery build + daily
SecretsFinds keys and passwords committed to gitgitleaks, GitHub secret scanningEvery push
DASTAttacks the running app from outsideZAP (now “ZAP by Checkmarx”), Burp SuiteNightly, on staging
FuzzingFeeds generated, malformed input to find crashesJazzer (coverage-guided, JUnit integration)Nightly / continuous
Pen testHumans think like attackersInternal or external security teamBefore big releases

Security tests you write yourself

OrderApiTest.java — hostile inputs✔ passes
@Test void pathTricksAreJustNotFound() throws Exception {
  for (String path : List.of("/orders/..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd",
                             "/orders/ord-1'%20OR%20'1'='1",
                             "/orders/" + "x".repeat(5_000))) {
    var res = send("GET", path);
    assertThat(res.statusCode()).isEqualTo(404);
    assertThat(res.body())               // no stack traces, no internals
        .isEqualTo("{\"error\":\"order not found\"}");
  }
}

Path traversal, SQL-looking IDs and a 5,000-character ID all get the same plain 404 — no stack trace, no SQL error, no file contents. This is a normal JUnit test; it runs on every build with the rest of the suite. The cards below are more ideas to turn into tests like this one.

Access controlUser A asks for /orders/{id} of user B → expect 403 or 404, never 200.
InjectionNames like ' OR 1=1 -- and <script> are stored and shown as plain text.
AuthenticationExpired, tampered and missing tokens all get 401; lock-out after repeated failures.
Input limitsHuge bodies, deep JSON, 10,000-item lists: rejected quickly, not crashing the server.
Error leakageErrors return a generic message — no stack traces, SQL or internal hostnames.
HeadersResponses with personal data send Cache-Control: no-store; HTTPS-only cookies.
Watch outBroken access control is A01, the first entry, in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (and was in 2021) — for example one user reading another’s data by changing an ID. A scanner does not know which user may see which record; write explicit tests for it on every endpoint that takes an ID.
Rule of thumbFail the build on new high-severity findings, and track the existing backlog separately, so that the first scan of an old code base does not block every build.

Resilience: test the failure, not just the success

TimeoutsPoint the client at a server that never answers; the call must give up in time.
Slow dependencyAdd latency with Toxiproxy (a Testcontainers module); check pools don’t exhaust.
Partial failureKill one instance or the cache during a load test; errors should stay bounded.
RetriesMake the dependency fail twice then succeed; assert exactly three calls and idempotent effects.

Chaos engineering takes the same idea to production-like environments: inject failures deliberately (kill pods, add latency) and check the system degrades the way you designed it to.

Testing in production: flags and synthetic checks

Tests before release can’t see the real network, data and load. Two habits make what happens after a deploy safer: every feature flag is tested both ways before it ships, and a synthetic check — the same code in a test and after every deploy — keeps asking “does it still work?”.

CheckoutPricingTest — both sides of the flag3 ✔ · 0.116 s
/** Every flag is two code paths: test both, every build. */
class CheckoutPricingTest {
  @ParameterizedTest(name = "flag={0}, {1} items → {2}")
  @CsvSource({
      "false, 3, 100000",
      "true,  3,  90000",
      "true,  2, 100000"})
  void bulkDiscountFollowsTheFlag(boolean on, int items,
      long total) {
    var pricing = new CheckoutPricing(new Features(on));
    assertThat(pricing.total(100_000, items)).isEqualTo(total);
  }
}
FeatureWiringTest — the property reaches the bean2 ✔ · 0.609 s
/** The property really reaches the bean; no web server, ~ms. */
class FeatureWiringTest {
  ApplicationContextRunner ctx = new ApplicationContextRunner()
      .withUserConfiguration(FeatureConfig.class);

  @Test
  void offWhenThePropertyIsMissing() {
    ctx.run(c -> assertThat(c.getBean(CheckoutPricing.class)
        .total(100_000, 3)).isEqualTo(100_000));
  }

  @Test
  void onWithThePropertySet() {
    ctx.withPropertyValues("shop.features.bulk-discount=true")
        .run(c -> assertThat(c.getBean(CheckoutPricing.class)
            .total(100_000, 3)).isEqualTo(90_000));
  }
}
SyntheticCheck.java — what a user does
public static List<String> run(URI base) {
  List<String> failures = new ArrayList<>();
  check(failures, base, "/actuator/health", "\"UP\"");
  check(failures, base, "/prices/book-1", "\"paise\"");
  return failures;
}

private static void check(List<String> failures, URI base,
    String path, String mustContain) {
  long t0 = System.nanoTime();
  String result;
  try {
    var req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(base.resolve(path))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
    var res = HTTP.send(req,
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
    boolean ok = res.statusCode() == 200
        && res.body().contains(mustContain);
    result = (ok ? "✔ " : "✘ ") + path
        + "  " + res.statusCode();
  } catch (Exception e) {
    result = "✘ " + path + "  "
        + e.getClass().getSimpleName();
  }
  long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000;
  System.out.println(result + "  " + ms + " ms");
  if (result.startsWith("✘")) {
    failures.add(result);
  }
}

  • Every flag is two code paths. Test both on every build; a flag that has been on everywhere for a release is deleted, with its tests.
  • One synthetic check, three places: the test above before the app ships, CI against the packaged jar, and production on a schedule after each deploy.
  • With Redis down the health endpoint said 503 and the check failed with exit code 1 — that is what pages someone.
Good to knowNot run here — practice: ship behind a flag that is off; turn it on for a canary (a small share of traffic); compare its error rate and latency with the old version; roll back automatically if they are worse; then turn it on for everyone.

Chapter six

Quality & process

Tests are only as useful as the habits around them: when you write them, how you know they are good enough, and how they run on every change. This chapter covers TDD, coverage, mutation testing, CI — and questions to check your understanding of all of it.

Test-driven development

Kent Beck’s Test-Driven Development: By Example (2002) describes a short loop: write a test for behaviour that doesn’t exist yet, watch it fail, write just enough code to pass, then improve the design while the tests stay green.

  • Red first proves the test can fail — a test that never failed may not test anything.
  • Simplest code that passes, even if it looks naive; the next test forces the real logic.
  • Refactor both code and tests; the tests are your safety net.

A real TDD loop: PasswordPolicy

step 1 · tests written, class just compiles
public class PasswordPolicy {
  public List<String> problems(String password) {
    return List.of();  // step 1: just enough to compile
  }
}

public class PasswordPolicy {
  public List<String> problems(String password) {
    List<String> problems = new ArrayList<>();
    if (password.length() < 12)
      problems.add("at least 12 characters");
    if (password.chars().noneMatch(Character::isDigit))
      problems.add("a digit");
    if (password.chars().noneMatch(Character::isUpperCase))
      problems.add("an upper-case letter");
    return problems;
  }
}

Step 3 · refactor: with all four green, we could pull the rules into a list of (predicate, message) pairs — and re-run to prove nothing changed.

Honest note: we wrote all four tests before the code, so three failed at once. Strict TDD adds one test at a time. The strong-password test passed even in the red step, because an empty list happens to be its right answer — a reminder to watch each new test fail before trusting it.

BDD: tests in the customer’s words

orders.feature · Gherkin example
Feature: Order discounts
  Scenario: Orders of ₹1000 or more get 5% off
    Given a cart with 2 books at ₹600 each
    When the customer places the order
    Then the order total is ₹1140.00
    And a confirmation e-mail is sent

Behaviour-driven development writes acceptance tests as Given / When / Then scenarios that product owners can read. Cucumber-JVM maps each line to a Java step method. Worth it when non-developers really read and write the scenarios; otherwise plain JUnit tests with good names are cheaper.

06 · Quality & process

Coverage & mutation testing

Code coverage (JaCoCo)

InstructionsC0Java bytecode instructions executed — the finest grain
BranchesC1Both outcomes of every if and switch case
LinesA line counts as covered when at least one of its instructions ran
ComplexityCyclomatic complexity: paths that would need tests
Methods / classesExecuted at least once

Coverage tells you what the tests ran, not what they checked. A test with no assertions can reach 100%. Use it to find untested code, not as a score to chase.

Mutation testing (PIT)

A tool changes your code in small ways — a mutant — and re-runs the tests. If they still pass, the mutant survived: your tests missed a bug. Mutation score = killed ÷ total. The idea goes back to Lipton (1971) and DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward (1978).

CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY< ↔ <=, >= ↔ >
NEGATE_CONDITIONALS== ↔ !=, < ↔ >=
MATH+ ↔ -, * ↔ /
INCREMENTSi++ ↔ i--
INVERT_NEGS-x → x
VOID_METHOD_CALLSremoves a call to a void method
…_RETURNSempty, null, true/false and 0 returns

A mutant, by hand: does the test suite notice?

WeakDiscountPolicyTest.java
/** 100% line + branch coverage, yet the bug survives. */
class WeakDiscountPolicyTest {
  DiscountPolicy policy = new DiscountPolicy();

  @Test void small() {
    assertEquals(0, policy.percentFor(Money.of("500")));
  }
  @Test void medium() {
    assertEquals(5, policy.percentFor(Money.of("2000")));
  }
  @Test void large() {
    assertEquals(10, policy.percentFor(Money.of("6000")));
  }
}
the mutant · CONDITIONALS_BOUNDARY
-    if (subtotal.compareTo(Money.of("1000")) >= 0) return 5;
+    if (subtotal.compareTo(Money.of("1000")) > 0) return 5;
weak tests vs MUTANT · real outputmutant survived
JUnit Jupiter
  '-- WeakDiscountPolicyTest [OK]
    +-- medium() [OK]
    +-- large() [OK]
    '-- small() [OK]
boundary tests (p.06) vs MUTANTmutant killed
JUnit Jupiter
  '-- DiscountPolicyTest [OK]
    '-- percentForSubtotal(String, int) [OK]
      +-- ₹0 → 0% off [OK]
      +-- ₹999.99 → 0% off [OK]
      +-- ₹1000 → 5% off [X] expected: <5> but was: <0>
      +-- ₹1000.01 → 5% off [OK]
      +-- ₹4999.99 → 5% off [OK]
      +-- ₹5000 → 10% off [OK]
      '-- ₹250000 → 10% off [OK]

The weak tests execute every line and both outcomes of each if, so line and branch coverage are both 100% — yet they let the bug through. The boundary test at exactly ₹1000 kills it. PIT does this automatically for thousands of mutants: mvn test-compile org.pitest:pitest-maven:mutationCoverage (pitest-maven 1.30.0, with the pitest-junit5-plugin for JUnit 5/6 tests).

Test smells to refactor away

SmellLooks likeFix
Assertion-free testCalls code, checks nothing — still counts as coverageAssert the outcome, or delete the test
Eager testOne test checks five behaviours; the name says “testOrder”Split it: one behaviour, one name
Mystery guestExpected values come from a file or DB row you can’t seeBuild the data inside the test (builders)
Fragile testBreaks on harmless refactors; verifies every internal callAssert results, not implementation steps
Sleepy testThread.sleep to wait for async workWait for a condition with a timeout
Rule of thumbRun mutation testing where it matters — pricing, permissions, money — or only on files changed in a pull request; it re-runs tests for every mutant, so it is slow.

Mutation testing with PIT: a worked run

We ran PIT 1.30.0 with pitest-junit5-plugin 1.2.3 on the shop example: every production class mutated with the DEFAULTS group, every unit and integration test run against each mutant. Below is what it found and how we fixed it.

Run 1 — what PIT reported

real PIT summary · run 139/40 detected
Line Coverage (for mutated classes only): 76/77 (99%)
22 tests examined
Generated 40 mutations Killed 39 (98%)
Mutations with no coverage 0. Test strength 98%

“22 tests examined” counts test classes; PIT ran each mutant against only the tests that cover its line. Run 2, after the fix: 40/40 detected — 100%. With the larger STRONGER group: 50/50 (100%).

Good to knowBefore writing a test for a survivor, ask whether the behaviour matters. Some mutants are equivalent — the change can’t alter any observable result — and no test can kill them. Accept those rather than writing a meaningless test.

The survivor

OrderApi.stop(), line 24: PIT deleted the call server.stop(0) and all 43 tests still passed. Nothing checked that stopping the API actually frees its port — a resource leak would ship unnoticed.

the test we added to kill it✔ passes
/** Kills the mutant PIT found: deleting server.stop(0). */
class OrderApiLifecycleTest {

  @Test void stopReleasesThePort() throws Exception {
    var api = new OrderApi(new InMemoryOrderRepository());
    int port = api.start();

    api.stop();

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> new Socket("127.0.0.1", port).close())
        .isInstanceOf(ConnectException.class);  // port is free
  }
}

Results by mutator

VOID_METHOD_CALLS105410
NEGATE_CONDITIONALS1010000
NULL_RETURNS77000

OrderApi · 24removed call to HttpServer::stop2KILLED (run 2)

Note what is not there: payments.charge(…) returns a value, so the DEFAULTS group never removes it — only void calls are removed. Larger groups (STRONGER, ALL) add mutators for those cases.

PIT in your build and CI

pom.xml — the same settings as our run, as Maven config
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
  <artifactId>pitest-maven</artifactId>
  <version>1.30.0</version>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>  <!-- runs JUnit 5/6 tests -->
      <groupId>org.pitest</groupId>
      <artifactId>pitest-junit5-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>1.2.3</version>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
  <configuration>
    <targetClasses><param>shop.*</param></targetClasses>
    <targetTests><param>shop.*Test</param></targetTests>
    <mutators><mutator>DEFAULTS</mutator></mutators>
    <mutationThreshold>90</mutationThreshold>  <!-- fail below 90% -->
    <coverageThreshold>85</coverageThreshold>
    <withHistory>true</withHistory>            <!-- incremental -->
    <threads>4</threads>
    <outputFormats><param>HTML</param><param>XML</param></outputFormats>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

Run it

CommandDoes
mvn test-compile pitest:mutationCoveragefull analysis; HTML report in target/pit-reports
-DtargetClasses=shop.pricing.*narrow the run to one package
-DwithHistoryreuse the last run’s results (incremental)
-Dmutators=STRONGERmore mutators; slower, finds more gaps

Making it fast enough for CI

  • Incremental: with history on, only changed code and tests are re-analysed.
  • Pull requests: PIT 1.30 has no git-diff goal. Narrow targetClasses to the changed module (or use Arcmutate’s commercial add-ons); run everything nightly.
  • Target it: modules with money, permissions and business rules first.
  • Our run: 31 s for 40 mutants on 2 CPUs, because PIT re-runs only the tests covering each mutant.

Reading a mutant’s status

StatusMeaningDetected?
KILLEDa test failed — the bug was caughtyes
TIMED_OUTmutant made the code hang (e.g. a removed start()); counted as detectedyes
SURVIVEDevery covering test still passed — a gap in your assertionsno
NO_COVERAGEno test even runs this lineno
NON_VIABLEthe mutated bytecode was invalid—
MEMORY_ERROR / RUN_ERRORthe test JVM crashedyes

Unit or integration tests?

PIT runs whatever tests you point it at. Ours included the HTTP integration tests, which is how it could detect mutants in OrderApi at all — no unit test touches that class. The cost: mutants that broke start() or the handler made tests hang until PIT’s timeout (the 4 TIMED_OUT results).

A practical split: run PIT on every pull request with unit tests only (fast, precise), and nightly with integration tests included for the modules where wiring matters. Keep those tests quick — random ports, fakes, no sleeps.

A workflow for survivors

1 · Read itOpen the HTML report: the line, the change PIT made, and which tests covered it.
2 · Does it matter?Would a user, caller or log notice the change? If not, it may be equivalent or the code may be dead.
3 · Test or deleteWrite the assertion that fails on the mutant — or delete code that nothing depends on.
4 · Gate the trendFail the build when the score drops below the threshold, so it can’t quietly erode.

Coverage for unit and integration tests

By default most builds measure coverage for unit tests only, so code exercised only by integration tests looks untested. We ran the JaCoCo 0.8.15 agent twice — once for the 39 unit tests, once for the 5 API integration tests — and merged the results (real numbers from coverage.sh; classes without branches left out).

Classunit
lines		IT
lines		merged
lines		unit
branches		IT
branches		merged
branches
OrderService100%0%100%100%0%100%
DiscountPolicy100%0%100%100%0%100%
Money100%42%100%100%50%100%

OrderApi0%100%100%0%100%100%
TOTAL69%49%100%80%30%100%
  • Unit tests alone: 69% of lines — OrderApi looks completely untested.
  • Integration tests alone: 49% — they never touch the pricing or password rules.
  • Merged: 100% of lines and branches. Each level covers what the other can’t.
  • Coverage is a floor, not a goal: PIT (p.40) is what showed the tests also check what they run.
pom.xml — unit + IT coverage, merged, with a gate
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.15</version>
  <configuration>  <!-- report and check read the merged file -->
    <dataFile>${project.build.directory}/jacoco-merged.exec</dataFile>
  </configuration>
  <executions>
    <execution><id>unit</id>      <!-- for Surefire -->
      <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>it</id>        <!-- for Failsafe -->
      <goals><goal>prepare-agent-integration</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>merge</id><phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>merge</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <fileSets><fileSet>
          <directory>${project.build.directory}</directory>
          <includes><include>jacoco.exec</include>
                    <include>jacoco-it.exec</include></includes>
        </fileSet></fileSets>
        <destFile>${project.build.directory}/jacoco-merged.exec</destFile>
      </configuration></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>gate</id><phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <rules><rule><element>BUNDLE</element><limits><limit>
          <counter>BRANCH</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
          <minimum>0.80</minimum>
        </limit></limits></rule></rules>
      </configuration></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

How the pieces fit

  • prepare-agent sets argLine for Surefire; prepare-agent-integration does the same for Failsafe, writing jacoco-it.exec.
  • merge combines the .exec files; report turns them into HTML, XML and CSV.
  • check fails the build when a rule isn’t met — here 80% of branches.
  • Multi-module builds: report-aggregate in a separate reporting module.
  • Other agents in argLine (like the Mockito agent on p.16) must keep JaCoCo’s value: write @{argLine} -javaagent:….
Rule of thumbGate coverage on new or changed code (SonarQube’s “new code” quality gate, or a diff-coverage tool) rather than the whole code base. Old, untested code then can’t block every merge, but nothing new arrives untested.

Finding duplicate & redundant tests

Two tests duplicate each other when they catch the same bugs. Run PIT with fullMutationMatrix=true — it records every test that kills each mutant — then compare the tests’ kill sets. The comparison is a small Java class with no dependencies; Maven or Gradle runs it right after PIT.

src/tools/shop/RedundantTests.java — comparing kill sets
List<String> tests = new ArrayList<>(kills.keySet());
tests.sort(Comparator.comparing((String t) -> -kills.get(t).size())
    .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
Map<Set<Integer>, List<String>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<>();
for (String t : tests)
  groups.computeIfAbsent(kills.get(t), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(t);
for (List<String> g : groups.values())
  if (g.size() > 1)
    System.out.println("  " + String.join("  ≡  ", g) + "   ("
        + kills.get(g.get(0)).size() + " mutants)");

for (String a : tests)
  for (String b : tests)
    if (!a.equals(b) && kills.get(b).containsAll(kills.get(a))
        && kills.get(b).size() > kills.get(a).size()) {
      System.out.printf("  %s (%d) ⊂ %s (%d)%n", a,
          kills.get(a).size(), b, kills.get(b).size());
      break;
    }

Equal kill sets mean the tests currently catch the same bugs — not that they are the same test. Delete only when the inputs are in the same partition and the assertions are the same.

A human verdict on each match

MatchWhat the tests areVerdict
ItemTest…rejected #1 ≡ #2 ≡ #3quantities 0, -1, MIN_VALUERedundant — same partition. Keep 0 (the boundary) and one negative.
DiscountPolicyTest #4 ≡ #5₹4999.99 and ₹5000Keep both — the two sides of a boundary.
PasswordPolicyTest digit ≡ upper-casetwo different rulesKeep both — they specify different rules.
OrderApiTest pathTricks ≡ unknownOrderboth expect 404Merge candidate — the hostile-input loop already covers the plain 404.
Unit test ⊂ OrderServiceTeste.g. MoneyTestKeep — a failing broad test doesn’t say which rule broke.

  • Both fail the build on duplicates. PMD’s UnitTestShouldIncludeAssert rule (left) finds tests that check nothing.
  • The Gradle CPD plugin (3.5, Nov 2024) prints Gradle 9 deprecation warnings.

Architecture tests with ArchUnit

Design rules written on a wiki erode one shortcut at a time. ArchUnit (Apache-2.0) turns them into JUnit tests over your compiled classes: a controller that reaches into a repository fails the build, with the exact line that broke the rule.

ArchitectureTest — ArchUnit 1.5.1, on the Spring project3 ✔ · 0.354 s
/** Design rules, checked on every build like any other test. */
@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "shop",
    importOptions = ImportOption.DoNotIncludeTests.class)
class ArchitectureTest {

  @ArchTest
  static final ArchRule CONTROLLERS_DONT_USE_REPOSITORIES =
      noClasses().that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Controller")
          .should().dependOnClassesThat()
          .haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Repository")
          .because("controllers go through a service");

  @ArchTest
  static final ArchRule CONTROLLERS_DONT_RETURN_ENTITIES =
      noClasses().that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Controller")
          .should().dependOnClassesThat()
          .areAnnotatedWith(Entity.class)
          .because("lazy JPA proxies must not reach JSON");

  @ArchTest
  static final ArchRule SERVICES_DONT_KNOW_THE_WEB =
      noClasses().that().haveSimpleNameEndingWith("Service")
          .should().dependOnClassesThat()
          .resideInAPackage("org.springframework.web..");
}
a deliberate violation (test sources only)
/** A deliberate violation, used to prove the rule bites. */
class ShortcutController {
  private final OrderRepository repository;

  ShortcutController(OrderRepository repository) {
    this.repository = repository;
  }

  long count() { return repository.count(); }
}
proving the rule bites1 ✔ · 0.877 s
  @Test
  void controllerCallingARepositoryIsReported() {
    var classes = new ClassFileImporter()
        .importPackages("shop.archdemo");

    assertThatThrownBy(() -> ArchitectureTest
        .CONTROLLERS_DONT_USE_REPOSITORIES.check(classes))
        .isInstanceOf(AssertionError.class)
        .hasMessageContaining("was violated (")
        .satisfies(e -> System.out.println(e.getMessage()));
  }
real output · the violation ArchUnit reported
Architecture Violation [Priority: MEDIUM] - Rule 'no classes that have simple name ending with 'Controller' should depend on classes that have simple name ending with 'Repository', because controllers go through a service' was violated (3 times):
Constructor <ShortcutController.<init>(OrderRepository)> has parameter of type <OrderRepository> in (ShortcutController.java:0)
Field <ShortcutController.repository> has type <OrderRepository> in (ShortcutController.java:0)
Method <ShortcutController.count()> calls method <OrderRepository.count()> in (ShortcutController.java:13)
  • Rules worth having: layer direction, no cycles between packages (slices().matching("..shop.(*)..").should().beFreeOfCycles()), naming, and “no java.util.Date” style bans.
  • Add .because(…) — the reason appears in the failure, so the next developer learns the rule instead of fighting it.
  • Prove each rule can fail once, as above; a rule with a typo in a package name passes forever.
  • Existing violations? FreezingArchRule records today’s and fails only on new ones — adopt rules without a big-bang clean-up.

No cycles between feature packagesslices().matching("..shop.(*)..").should().beFreeOfCycles()
Domain code stays framework-freenoClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("org.springframework..")

Parallel tests: threads for unit, JVMs for integration

Unit tests share nothing, so they run as threads in one JVM. Integration tests share heavy, stateful resources — a database, a container, a port — so they run in several JVMs, each with its own copy of those resources.

Unit testsIntegration tests
Run side by side asthreads in one JVMseparate JVM processes (forks)
What tests sharenothing — objects live in memorycontainers, ports, database rows, Spring context, files
Configure withJUnit junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.*Failsafe forkCount; Gradle maxParallelForks
Isolation comes fromno shared mutable state; @ResourceLock for the resteach fork has its own JVM, singletons and data
Cost of one morea thread — almost freea JVM start and its own containers
Usual settingon, for every builda few forks — measure, don’t guess (p.47)
pom.xml — Surefire threads, Failsafe forks
<!-- UNIT tests: one JVM, many threads -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.6.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <properties>
      <configurationParameters>
        junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true
        junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = concurrent
        junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default = concurrent
      </configurationParameters>
    </properties>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

<!-- INTEGRATION tests: many JVMs, one singleton container each -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.6.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <forkCount>${it.forks}</forkCount>
    <reuseForks>true</reuseForks>
    <!-- -Dfork=1, 2, ...: which fork this JVM is -->
    <argLine>@{argLine} -Xshare:off -Dfork=${surefire.forkNumber}
             -javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}</argLine>
  </configuration>
  ...
</plugin>
build.gradle.kts — Gradle forks
// INTEGRATION tests: many JVMs, one singleton container each
val integrationTest = tasks.register<Test>("integrationTest") {
  description = "Runs *IT classes in parallel JVMs"
  group = "verification"
  testClassesDirs = sourceSets["integrationTest"].output.classesDirs
  classpath = sourceSets["integrationTest"].runtimeClasspath
  useJUnitPlatform()
  maxParallelForks = 2
  shouldRunAfter(tasks.test)
  testLogging { showStandardStreams = true }
}
tasks.check { dependsOn(integrationTest) }
  • forkCount=2 runs up to two test JVMs at once; 2C means two per CPU core. reuseForks=true (the default) keeps each JVM for many classes, so its singletons start once.
  • ${surefire.forkNumber} becomes 1…forkCount. Our run: a system property that was only the placeholder arrived empty, while shop_${surefire.forkNumber} and argLine worked. Print it once.
  • Surefire’s own parallel parameter is for JUnit 4 and TestNG; for JUnit Jupiter pass JUnit’s settings, as above.
  • Gradle: maxParallelForks (default 1). Each worker gets a unique org.gradle.test.worker property — unique, but not 1…N: our runs got workers 2 and 3.
  • reuseForks=false (Maven) or forkEvery (Gradle) recycles JVMs — for leaky tests only; singletons restart too.
  • Maven’s -T (parallel modules) multiplies the forks: 3 modules × forkCount=2 can mean 6 JVMs and 6 containers.

06 · Quality & process

Singleton containers: one per test JVM

Testcontainers’ documented pattern for sharing a container is the singleton container: a static field in a base class, started in a static initialiser. It starts once when the first subclass loads, every IT class in that JVM reuses it, and the Ryuk container removes it when the JVM exits. With forks: one container per fork.

src/it/java/shop/SharedPostgres.java (Testcontainers 2.0.5)
abstract class SharedPostgres {
  static final String FORK = System.getProperty("fork",
      System.getProperty("org.gradle.test.worker", "1"));
  static final PostgreSQLContainer DB =
      new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine");

  static {
    DB.start();                 // once per JVM, never stop() here
    // … create the schema, log the container id
  }

  static Connection connect() throws SQLException {
    return DriverManager.getConnection(
        DB.getJdbcUrl(), DB.getUsername(), DB.getPassword());
  }
  // log(), uniqueId(), insert() …
}
an IT class just extends it
class OrderKeyIT extends SharedPostgres {
  @BeforeAll static void hello() {
    log("OrderKeyIT uses " + DB.getJdbcUrl());
  }

  @Test void duplicateIdIsRejected() throws Exception {
    String id = uniqueId("dup");
    try (var c = connect()) {
      insert(c, id, "10");
      assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(c, id, "20"))
          .isInstanceOf(SQLException.class)
          .extracting(e -> ((SQLException) e).getSQLState())
          .isEqualTo("23505");          // unique_violation
    }
  }
}
Watch outDon’t annotate the singleton with @Container and don’t call stop(): the JUnit extension stops a static @Container after the last test of its class, so the next class would find it gone.

Real run: Failsafe, forkCount=2, Docker on GitHub Actions

Apache Maven 3.10.0 · Failsafe 3.6.0 · 2 containers for 4 database IT classes10 tests ✔
[fork 1 pid 2665] Postgres 2d7f090afddf on port 32771
[fork 1 pid 2665] OrderTableIT uses port 32771
[fork 2 pid 2666] Postgres f761dd55aa56 on port 32770
[fork 2 pid 2666] OrderKeyIT uses port 32770
  ✔ OrderKeyIT — 6.480 s
[fork 2 pid 2666] OrderSearchIT uses port 32770
  ✔ OrderTableIT — 7.083 s
  ✔ OrderSearchIT — 0.074 s
  • One container per JVM. Fork 1 started a container for OrderKeyIT (6.5 s, mostly start-up); OrderSearchIT reused it and took 0.07 s. Fork 2 started its own for OrderTableIT.
  • Measure it. Same build, warm Docker, two runs each on a 4-CPU runner: one IT JVM 15.2–15.3 s, two JVMs 19.1–19.6 s for the whole mvn verify. Two forks were slower here: two containers start at once on a small machine and our tests are short. Forks pay off when IT classes run for minutes.
  • Spring: the context cache is per JVM too, so each fork builds its own context; wire the container in with @DynamicPropertySource.
  • Gradle with maxParallelForks = 2: the same, one container per worker.

06 · Quality & process

Faster builds: build cache & test shards

When the suite gets slow, don’t delete tests — stop re-running what didn’t change, and split what must run across machines. Both below are real runs on GitHub Actions.

1 · Build cache: skip unchanged work

real output · clean test, without and with the cache
### gradle clean test --no-build-cache
> Task :compileJava
> Task :compileTestJava
> Task :testClasses
> Task :test
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 5s
4 actionable tasks: 4 executed
### gradle clean test --build-cache
> Task :compileJava FROM-CACHE
> Task :compileTestJava FROM-CACHE
> Task :testClasses UP-TO-DATE
> Task :test FROM-CACHE
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 858ms
4 actionable tasks: 1 executed, 3 from cache
  • Gradle hashes every task’s inputs — sources, dependencies, JVM arguments. With --build-cache (or org.gradle.caching=true), a task whose inputs were seen before is restored FROM-CACHE instead of run — tests included.
  • Real run: 5s with the cache off, every task executed; 858ms with it on — compiled classes and test results came from the cache that gradle/actions/setup-gradle keeps between CI runs.
  • Share a remote cache between CI and laptops so a branch built once is cheap everywhere.
  • Maven has no built-in build cache; the Apache Maven Build Cache Extension adds one.

2 · Shards: split test classes across machines

.github/workflows/build.yml — two shards
  shard:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix: { shard: [1, 2] }       # two machines, half the classes each
    defaults: { run: { shell: 'bash -eo pipefail {0}' } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '21' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6
      - name: Run this shard's test classes
        run: |
          mkdir -p logs
          classes=$(cd src/test/java && find . -name '*Test.java' \
            | sed 's#^./##; s#.java$##; s#/#.#g' | sort \
            | awk -v n=2 -v k=${{ matrix.shard }} 'NR % n == k % n')
          echo "shard ${{ matrix.shard }}/2: $(echo $classes | wc -w) classes" | tee logs/shard.log
          ./gradlew --console=plain test $(printf -- '--tests %s ' $classes) 2>&1 | tail -3 | tee -a logs/shard.log
          # … then count the tests this shard ran
  • Real run: shard 1 ran 23 tests and shard 2 ran 21 — all 44, on two machines at once.
  • Split by class, never by method: @BeforeAll setup and shared fixtures stay together.
  • Balance by duration, not count, once the suite grows: the slowest shard decides the total time.
  • Collect every shard’s JUnit XML report in one place, so a failure is visible without opening each job.

TechniqueHowWatch out

Parallel forksthreads for unit tests, forks for ITs (p.46)measure first — it was slower for us
Test selectionrun only tests affected by a change (e.g. Develocity Predictive Test Selection, commercial)keep a full run nightly

Run tests in parallel

junit-platform.properties

junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default=concurrent

Our 44 tests on 4 CPUs, three runs each: sequential 1,979–2,032 ms, parallel 1,444–1,475 ms, all passing. Parallel runs only work if tests share no state — a good test of your tests.

.github/workflows/build.yml · sketchnot run here
name: build
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '21', cache: maven }
      - run: ./mvnw -B verify   # unit + integration
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()            # keep reports on failure
        with: { name: test-reports, path: '**/target/*-reports/*.xml' }

Pipeline habits

  • Fastest first. Static checks and unit tests run before anything slow, so most failures arrive in minutes.
  • Every pull request runs the full unit and integration suite; merging is blocked on red.
  • Keep reports (JUnit XML, coverage, Playwright traces) as build artefacts, especially on failure.
  • Budget the time. If the main build creeps past ~10 minutes, parallelise, split jobs or push slow suites to nightly.
  • Quarantine flaky tests in a non-blocking job and fix them — never “retry until green”.
  • Show results in the pull request: test, coverage and mutation summaries next to the diff get read; a link to a dashboard doesn’t.

Four questions for every test in code review

Would it fail?If the behaviour broke, would this test go red? (PIT answers this for you.)
Right level?Is it the lowest level that can catch the bug — unit before integration before end-to-end?
Readable?Does the name state the expected behaviour, and does a failure message say what went wrong?
Independent?No shared state, real time, sleeps or test order; safe to run in parallel.

06 · Quality & process

Check your understanding

Twenty questions to check your understanding — for self-review, team discussions or onboarding. Each has a short answer to start from; the index points to the page that covers the topic in depth.

Q01Unit vs integration test?

A unit test checks one class with its collaborators replaced, in memory and in milliseconds. An integration test checks your code together with real parts — database, HTTP, framework — and is slower but catches wiring and configuration bugs.

Q02Mock vs stub?

A stub returns canned answers so the code under test can run; you then check the result (state). A mock is set up with expectations about calls, which you verify (behaviour). Mockito objects can play either role.

Q03What does @InjectMocks do?

Creates the class under test and injects @Mock/@Spy fields by constructor, then setter, then field. It fails silently when it can’t inject — many teams prefer calling the constructor explicitly.

Q04when().thenReturn() vs doReturn().when()?

Use doReturn for spies (the when form calls the real method first) and doThrow/doNothing for void methods.

Q05How do you test a private method?

Through the public method that uses it. If that is too hard, the private logic probably wants to be its own class with its own tests.

Q06How do you test code that uses the current time?

Inject a java.time.Clock; production passes Clock.systemUTC(), tests pass Clock.fixed(…).

Q07What is a flaky test and how do you fix it?

One that passes and fails without code changes. Find the uncontrolled input — time, randomness, order, shared state, network, sleeps — and control it; quarantine until fixed.

Q08Is 100% coverage the goal?

No. Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked. Use it to find untested code; use mutation testing to judge test strength.

Q09@BeforeEach vs @BeforeAll?

@BeforeEach runs before every test on a fresh instance; @BeforeAll runs once per class and must be static unless @TestInstance(PER_CLASS).

Q10Can Mockito mock final classes and statics?

Yes. Since Mockito 5 the inline mock maker is the default, so final classes and methods work; statics need mockStatic in a try-with-resources block.

Q11What is the test pyramid?

Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests — because cost and flakiness grow as tests get broader. The testing trophy puts more weight on integration tests.

Q12How do you test a REST controller in Spring Boot?

@WebMvcTest with MockMvcTester (or MockMvc) and @MockitoBean services for the web layer; @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT) plus Testcontainers for a full flow.

Q13What is TDD and when is it worth it?

Red–green–refactor in short loops. Most valuable for logic with clear rules (pricing, parsing, validation); less so for exploratory UI work.

Q14How do you test exceptions in JUnit?

assertThrows(Type.class, () -> …) returns the exception so you can check its message; AssertJ offers assertThatThrownBy(…). Avoid the JUnit 4 @Test(expected = …) style — it passes if any line throws.

Q15What is mutation testing?

A tool (PIT) makes small changes to your code — flips >= to >, removes a call — and re-runs the tests. Surviving mutants show where tests run code without really checking it.

Q16How do you make tests run in parallel safely?

Remove shared mutable state: no statics, unique test data, temp dirs, random ports. Then enable junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled; use @ResourceLock for anything truly shared.

Q17Surefire vs Failsafe?

Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase (*Test). Failsafe runs integration tests (*IT) in integration-test and fails the build in verify, so clean-up still happens.

Q18What do you test in a microservice architecture?

Each service with unit and integration tests, the agreements between services with contract tests, and only a few critical journeys end to end.

Q19How do you find duplicate or redundant tests?

Run PIT with the full mutation matrix and compare which mutants each test kills; equal sets are merge candidates. Add copy-paste detection (PMD CPD, SonarQube) and review — boundary tests often look redundant but aren’t.

Q20What is contract testing?

Consumers publish the requests and responses they rely on; the provider’s build verifies them (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract). It replaces many slow end-to-end tests between services.

@BeforeAll / @AfterAllonce per class (static)

assertEquals(exp, act)expected first
assertThrows(X.class, …)returns the exception

Mockito
when(m.f()).thenReturn(v)stub
doReturn(v).when(spy).f()stub a spy
doThrow(e).when(m).voidF()stub a void
verify(m).f(eq(1), any())all matchers or none
verify(m, never()).f()not called
verifyNoInteractions(m)untouched
@Captor ArgumentCaptor<T>grab the argument
mockStatic(X.class)try-with-resources
Test doubles
  • Dummy — fills a parameter, never used
  • Stub — canned answers
  • Spy — stub that records calls
  • Mock — expectations, verified
  • Fake — working shortcut (in-memory repo)
Which level?
  • Unit — rules, calculations, orchestration
  • Integration — SQL, HTTP, JSON, config
  • Contract — agreements between services
  • End-to-end — a few money-making journeys
  • Push each check to the cheapest level that catches it
Flaky? Control the input
  • Time → inject Clock
  • Random → seed it
  • Sleep → wait for a condition
  • Shared state → fresh fixtures, unique IDs
  • Network → stub or container
Commands
mvn testunit tests (Surefire)
mvn verify+ integration tests (Failsafe)
mvn test -Dtest=MoneyTestone class
mvn test -Dtest='MoneyTest#rejects*'matching methods
mvn test -Dgroups=fastonly @Tag("fast")
./gradlew test --tests '*MoneyTest'Gradle filter
mvn test-compile pitest:mutationCoveragemutation testing (PIT)
target/site/jacoco/index.htmlJaCoCo report after mvn verify
Golden rules
  • Watch every new test fail first
  • One behaviour per test, named as a sentence
  • Arrange · Act · Assert — and nothing else
  • Test behaviour through the public API
  • Don’t mock values or what you don’t own
  • Boundaries: test on and either side of every edge
  • Coverage finds gaps; PIT measures strength — merge unit + IT coverage
  • A flaky test is a bug — quarantine and fix it
Versions used here
  • JUnit 6.1.3 · Java 17+
  • Mockito 5.24.0 · AssertJ 3.27.7
  • Run on OpenJDK 21
Performance
  • Report p50 / p95 / p99, not the mean
  • Warm up the JVM before measuring
  • Little’s Law: users = rate × time
Security in CI
  • SAST + SCA + secrets on every build
  • DAST (ZAP) nightly on staging
  • Write access-control tests yourself
